item.title: Chris Van Hollen to challenge Schumer for Senate majority leader
item.description:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen announced Thursday that he'll challenge Chuck Schumer for majority leader.

Why it matters: Van Hollen's bid gives grassroots activists nearly three weeks to pressure Senate Democrats before they cast secret ballots in the Dec. 1 leadership election.

  • The attempt to oust Schumer (D-N.Y.) underscores that deep divisions are plaguing the Democratic Party despite its overwhelming midterm success.
  • Van Hollen (D-Md.) has served in the Senate since 2017 and has been in Congress since 2003.
  • Schumer has been the Senate Democratic leader since 2017 and has served in the Senate since 1999.

Driving the news: "In this election, the American people called for change," Van Hollen said in a statement on Thursday.

  • "They called for a change from Donald Trump's disastrous policies — but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn't working for working people." "It's now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person — it's about answering the call of the American people. That is why I'm running for Senate Majority Leader."
  • In a statement of his own, Schumer said: "I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic leader."

Zoom in: Van Hollen acknowledged he's the "underdog" in the race but claimed Thursday on MS NOW he has "more than 10" senators on his side.

  • "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who demanded a plan for change from party leadership.
  • Progressives have accused Schumer of not fighting hard enough against President Trump and the MAGA agenda.
  • Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.) is a vocal backer of Van Hollen for majority leader.

The other side: Schumer has far more public backers at this stage than Van Hollen.

  • That includes Sen. Angus King (I-Maine), Sen.-elect Sherrod Brown (Ohio) and Democratic Sens. John Fetterman (Pa.), Ruben Gallego (Ariz.), Kirsten Gillibrand (N.Y.), Mark Kelly (Ariz.), Jacky Rosen (Nev.), Brian Schatz (Hawaii) and Sheldon Whitehouse (Rhode Island).

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and has been updated.

item.title: House Democratic leaders face fallout over poorly timed floor vote fumbles
item.description:
A week that was supposed to see House Democrats transition seamlessly from a landslide midterm victory to a leadership coronation has instead been pocked by surprise Republican victories on the House floor.

Why it matters: Skeptics of Democratic leadership have seized on these strategic fumbles to cast doubt on their much-heralded managerial abilities in the lead-up to the party's leadership elections next week.

  • "It's really unfortunate that this happened this week when, obviously, that is a narrative we hear leadership portray," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.) told Axios.
  • Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) said this week has "certainly not given me confidence," and that the election was an "indictment on how our party has been operating thus far, and this is a big part of why."
  • "We do know that the Democratic caucus has blundered before on things, like whipping the votes to protect NPR last spring," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "We botched that one."

What happened: The House voted 211 to 204 on Tuesday to quash an effort by Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) to impeach Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, with support from all House Democrats present.

  • The outcome quickly sparked backlash because nearly a dozen House Democrats were absent, many of whom got caught in a traffic jam returning from an Elect Democratic Women event.
  • That was followed by an incident on Wednesday in which House Republicans passed a veterans bill by voice vote despite Democratic opposition.
  • The incidents follow a procedural blowup in September in which a pair of centrist House Democrats repeatedly broke with leadership and helped the GOP advance key bills.

What they're saying: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), asked about these incidents by Axios, touted a different veterans bill Democrats forced to a successful floor vote on Thursday via a discharge petition.

  • "House Democrats once again successfully forced a vote on a piece of legislation designed to make life better for the American people," he said.
  • House Minority Whip Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) did not respond to Axios' question and walked off the House floor into her office.

The intrigue: Even some current and incoming House Democrats who are voting for Jeffries as speaker acknowledged the vote was a black eye.

  • "I think everyone's frustrated with how that all went down, I'm not going to lie to you about that," said Rep.-elect Dan Koh (D-Mass.).
  • "People are pissed," a senior House Democrat told Axios.

The other side: Other Democrats told Axios the absences were an inevitable reality of Congress, noting that several who missed votes have said they were attending to emergencies.

  • "I think everyone's explained what the situations were — somebody was recovering from surgery. There are certain things that are unavoidable," said Rep. Adelita Grijalva (D-Ariz.).
  • Others said the upshot is that House Democrats need to do a better job of getting to votes on time: "The general consensus among the new members is on Jan. 3, it's time to lock in," Rep.-elect Matt Little (D-Minn.) told Axios.

Others said the speakership election offers a window into how Jeffries' approach to the speakership might play out over the coming year.

  • Jeffries has always taken a more hands-off approach than his predecessor, former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.), preferring to let issues and fights among members resolve themselves.

item.title: Senate Dems can look forward to unlikely MAGA allies
item.description:
Senate Democrats could find some of their most surprising allies next Congress from the right wing of the Republican Party.

Why it matters: Senate Democrats are on track to need only four GOP votes to break filibusters next Congress. They could find those votes from a bloc of GOP senators with a shared appetite for taking on corporate power.

  • Enter Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), Jim Banks (R-Ind.), Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) and Eric Schmitt (R-Mo.).
  • Each has already worked with Democrats, and their votes could put legislation over the top.

Who we're watching: Hawley has co-led multiple pieces of legislation with progressive star Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) this Congress.

  • Hawley is often viewed as a loner in the GOP, pairing populist economics with hardcore culture war issues from abortion to transgender care to religious freedom.
  • He's been scathing in his postelection critiques. "This Congress did not come and work for the people. This Congress came and worked for AI companies, and it worked for data centers, and it worked for big tech companies," he told reporters on Tuesday.
  • He's scoping out areas for potential bipartisan deals: "You want to raise the minimum wage? I'm for that. You want to work to get gas prices down? I'm for that. I am open to anything to bring down the cost of health care," he said.

Zoom in: Watch the health care space, specifically undoing cuts passed in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and drug price controls.

  • President Trump has specifically asked Congress to codify his most favored nations drug pricing deals, which could give Republicans an opening to work with Democrats.
  • Hawley and moderate Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) were among the loudest GOP voices opposing the expiration of enhanced Affordable Care Act credits last year.

Zoom out: Social Security and tech safety issues could also be huge areas of unexpected bipartisan work.

  • Over the summer, Warren and Moreno released a sweeping plan to "save Social Security."
  • Warren and Banks have tag-teamed on numerous tech and AI safety bills, including a joint statement on Nvidia this week. Hawley is also a major critic of AI.
  • Schmitt worked with Warren in 2024 and 2025 to challenge Big Tech's dominance of Pentagon AI contracts, and with Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) in July to crack down on search engine monopolies.

What to watch: While there will be fewer this Congress, Democrats will also have a club of more moderate Republicans they can try to pick up too.

  • Murkowski, along with Sens. John Curtis (R-Utah) and Todd Young (R-Ind.), will be top targets.

item.title: 11 names to watch in the Jensen Huang succession search
item.description:
Data: Photos: Getty Images, Nvidia, Apple; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios

Nvidia has begun searching for a permanent replacement for longtime CEO Jensen Huang, who resigned Thursday amid scrutiny over reports of multiple extramarital affairs.

Why it matters: Nvidia's next leader will inherit one of the world's most valuable companies — and the daunting task of succeeding the pioneer who transformed it into an AI powerhouse.

  • The job will require as much political savvy as technological expertise, Axios' Nathan Bomey says. The next CEO must navigate regulatory scrutiny, geopolitical tensions and the economic upheaval unleashed by the AI boom.

Catch up quick: Nvidia announced Thursday that CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO following Huang's departure.

  • The board said it would consider both internal and external candidates. Longtime director Harvey Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair following Huang's departure.

Reality check: Huang never publicly named a successor, leaving investors and analysts to speculate about who could take the helm.

  • In an October Bloomberg interview released Thursday, Huang said he hoped Nvidia's next CEO was already working at the company.

Here are 11 names that have surfaced in reporting and speculation — from leading contenders to long shots.

Colette Kress

Colette Kress, the new interim CEO of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia bio page

Kress could stay on permanently, with analysts and investors viewing her as a leading contender because of her financial expertise, per Reuters. Nvidia's new board chair, Harvey Jones, praised Kress for her deep understanding of the company's business and customers.

  • Kress has represented Nvidia on investor calls for more than a decade, making her one of the company's most recognizable executives.
  • She's also the only person, aside from Huang, who had much visibility across the company, according to Axios' Ina Fried. Huang had several dozen direct reports, many of whom oversaw relatively narrow parts of the business.

Yes, but: Her finance background could raise doubts about whether she could match Huang's technological prowess.

Ian Buck

Ian Buck of Nvidia. Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets

Buck is among the potential successors drawing attention from analysts and investors, Reuters reported, given his engineering expertise and prominent position inside Nvidia.

  • He currently serves as Nvidia's vice president and general manager of hyperscale and high-performance computing.
  • He also helped develop CUDA, Nvidia's computing platform that made its graphics processors essential to modern AI development.

Chris Malachowsky

Photo illustration: Axios Visuals. Photo: Nvidia media assets

Malachowsky co-founded Nvidia with Huang in 1993 and helped shape the company's technology over the next three decades, according to his Nvidia bio page.

  • "Malachowsky has been instrumental in managing, defining and driving the company's core technologies as it has grown from a startup to the global leader in accelerated computing," the page reads.
  • Much of his background is in engineering and technical leadership.

Yes, but: His role today is less focused on day-to-day company management, raising questions about whether he would want to assume the CEO position.

René Haas

Arm CEO Rene Haas at the Nasdaq MarketSite in New York on Sept. 14, 2023. Photo: Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Haas, the CEO of British chip designer Arm Holdings, has emerged as an outside contender because of his chip industry experience and previous work at Nvidia, per multiple reports.

  • He's a former Nvidia executive who has the public-facing skills that may be required as Nvidia faces heavy scrutiny from investors and government probes.
  • Nvidia uses Arm's processor technology in some products.

Flashback: Nvidia previously tried to acquire Arm in a $40 billion deal, but the companies abandoned the transaction in 2022 amid significant regulatory opposition.

Tim Cook

President Trump and Apple CEO Tim Cook shake hands in the Oval Office at the White House. Photo: Win McNamee/Getty Images

Former Apple CEO Tim Cook's name entered the succession conversation Thursday after President Trump publicly suggested he take over Nvidia.

  • Cook's high profile and experience running one of the world's largest technology companies have fueled speculation that he could be a dark horse.
  • Cook has also been mentioned in prediction market speculation.

Yes, but: It's unclear whether Cook would want the job after recently stepping down as Apple's CEO.

Johny Srouji

Johny Srouji appears on a laptop screen during Apple's 2020 virtual Worldwide Developers Conference, viewed in Arlington, Va. Photo: Andrew Harrer/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Bloomberg has identified Srouji, Apple's chief hardware officer, as another potential successor.

  • Before that, he led the development of Apple's custom chips for the iPhone, Mac and other Apple devices.

Nikesh Arora

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora attends the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi, India in Feb. 2026. Photo: Prakash Singh/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Arora, the CEO of Palo Alto Networks, has emerged as a potential successor, with The Economic Times reporting investors have floated his name.

  • Arora has led Palo Alto Networks since 2018 and overseen the company's expansion into AI-powered cybersecurity.
  • He previously served as president and chief operating officer of SoftBank and worked for a decade at Google, per his official biography.

Yes, but: His experience is largely in cybersecurity and other areas of tech, rather than chip development.

Lisa Su

AMD CEO Lisa Su speaks onstage during the company's Gamers Day 2026 event in Seoul, South Korea. Photo: SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Su has led AMD, one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, for more than a decade. Bloomberg identified her as a potential successor given her deep experience in the chip industry.

Yes, but: Su already runs one of Nvidia's biggest rivals, and she was just named "CEO of the Year" by Yahoo! Finance.

  • Axios chief technology correspondent Ina Fried says Su might relish competing with a weakened Nvidia rather than taking over for Huang.

Thomas Kurian

Thomas Kurian speaks onstage during Oracle's OpenWorld conference in San Francisco in 2017. Photo: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Kurian, the CEO of Google Cloud could also be considered.

  • Kurian oversees cloud infrastructure, enterprise software and AI services, giving him experience with major customers and technology essential to Nvidia's business.

Yes, but: His resume does not feature chip design experience.

Pat Gelsinger

Former Intel CEO Pat Gelsinger holds up a processor while speaking onstage at the Computex technology conference in Taipei in 2024. Photo: Annabelle Chih/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The former Intel CEO boasts decades of semiconductor engineering and leadership experience at one of Nvidia's longtime competitors.

  • Gelsinger has publicly criticized Nvidia's approach to AI computing, backed its competitors and sparred with Huang over the future of chips.

Yes, but: Gelsinger struggled to make Intel a stronger AI competitor. His name has surfaced in online speculation, but there's no public indication Nvidia's board is considering him.

Madison Huang

Nvidia executives Madison Huang (left) and Spencer Huang attend a company event at the site of Nvidia's planned Constellation campus in Taipei in May 2026. Photo: An Rong Xu/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Huang's daughter Madison has emerged as a possible long-term successor, according to reporting by the Financial Times, citing sources familiar.

  • She's a senior director working on product marketing for Nvidia's physical AI business and has been described as a rising star within the company. Her name has also surfaced in prediction market speculation.

Zoom in: Huang's son Spencer and son-in-law Nico Caprez also work at Nvidia. Caprez, who oversees global AI infrastructure growth, has also been tapped as a potential successor, per Bloomberg.

Yes, but: Huang's children hold relatively junior positions compared with Nvidia's more experienced executives.

  • Asked about his daughter's potential succession in the Bloomberg interview, Huang said Madison and her brother Spencer would have to earn the position rather than inherit it.

item.title: Logan Circle gunman shot 4 from balcony, started fire, police say
item.description:
A gunman killed one person inside a Logan Circle gym and shot four others from his apartment balcony Thursday morning, before setting a fire and fatally shooting himself, police say.

The big picture: The shooting triggered a massive law enforcement response in one of D.C.'s busiest neighborhoods, prompting residents to shelter in place and nearly a dozen nearby schools to go into lockdown.

The latest: At an afternoon press conference, interim MPD chief Jeffery W. Carroll identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Wade Lambert, who lived in the apartment building connected to VIDA Fitness, where police say he fatally shot one person.

  • The man killed was 46-year-old James Stuart, the building's manager and a Northwest D.C. resident, Carroll said.
  • Police believe the shooting was linked to an ongoing dispute between Lambert and his condominium association over maintenance issues, including mold. Lambert had filed a lawsuit against the association in March 2025.

What we know: Police responded to a shooting inside VIDA Fitness, at 15th and P streets NW, just before 8am. Additional reports of shootings nearby followed within minutes.

  • The victims: Stuart was pronounced dead inside VIDA. Two men and two women were hospitalized after being shot outside, Carroll said. One remains in critical condition; the other three sustained non-life-threatening injuries.
  • The shooter: Police say Lambert shot Stuart inside the gym with a handgun before returning to his apartment in the same building, where he fired at four people below from an upper-level private balcony.
  • The standoff: MPD reported a barricade situation in the 1500 block of 15th Street NW. Lambert barricaded himself in his seventh-floor apartment and fired twice through the door at responding officers, Carroll said. None were injured.
  • The fire: Lambert broke a gas line connected to his fireplace and started a fire inside the apartment, Carroll said. Flames were visible outside the building, but sprinklers helped contain the blaze. Police recovered gasoline and other flammable materials.
  • The weapons: Investigators recovered a handgun, shotgun and rifle from Lambert's apartment. Carroll said the suspect used all three firearms, none of which were registered in D.C.

Police negotiators heard a gunshot while speaking with Lambert by phone, after which he stopped responding. Tactical officers forced entry and found him suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

  • MPD announced around 11:10am that the barricade had ended and the scene was safe.
People stand behind police tape in Logan Circle early Thursday. Photo: Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Zoom out: The huge law enforcement response blocked off nearby streets and the neighborhood Whole Foods.

  • Nearly a dozen DC Public Schools in the vicinity, from Columbia Heights to Adams Morgan, went into lockdown, and later resumed activity before noon.
  • Police helicopters circled overhead throughout the morning, rattling windows in surrounding neighborhoods.
  • Carroll said the shootings themselves likely unfolded in less than five minutes, though investigators are still reconstructing the timeline.
A U.S. Park Police helicopter flies above the scene. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
U.S. Marshal officers move position at the scene of the Logan Circle shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images
Residents cross a street as law enforcement responds to the shooting. Photo: Andrew Harnik/Getty Images

What we don't know: Police have not determined whether Lambert knew the four surviving victims or deliberately targeted them.

  • The precise timeline and extent of the suspected planning also remain under investigation.

Context: The shooting prompted a massive response from local and federal authorities, including MPD, D.C. Fire and EMS, U.S. Park Police, Metro Transit Police and other federal law enforcement agencies.

  • Asked whether the show of force was due to the shooting's proximity to the White House, roughly a mile away, Carroll said it was because police were responding to an active shooter. "The expectation is folks will go there to try to stop the loss of life," he said. Mayor Bowser confirmed the White House had been briefed.
  • President Trump has surged federal law enforcement in D.C. through his Safe and Beautiful Task Force. In a speech before the midterms last week, Trump declared D.C. "one of the safest cities in the country."
  • Asked about Trump's role in reducing crime during Thursday's morning briefing, Bowser pushed back: "I praise MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors."

This is a developing story. Check back for details.

item.title: Scott Colom's win in Mississippi puts political change to the test
item.description:
Mississippi, a state with the largest share of Black residents in the country, has elected its first Black U.S. senator in nearly 150 years.

Why it matters: For generations, Black Mississippians left the state to escape Jim Crow and pursue economic and political opportunities elsewhere.

  • Now, Mississippi faces a new question: Was Scott Colom's victory a once-in-a-generation breakthrough, or the beginning of an era of Black political power?

Driving the news: Colom's defeat of incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith broke a barrier that had stood since Reconstruction.

  • Mississippi was the first state to send Black senators to Congress, before violence and disenfranchisement stripped Black residents of their political power.
  • In Colom's race, Democrats gained ground in 75 of the state's 82 counties, Marvin King, an associate professor of political science and African American studies at the University of Mississippi, told Axios.
  • "It wasn't just a fluke of super high turnout in one particular region," he said. "Scott Colom's victory can signal that maybe Mississippi is ready to govern differently."

The big picture: During the Great Migration, roughly 6 million Black Americans left the South to escape discrimination and seek better opportunities.

  • Many Black Mississippians built political power in Northern cities such as Chicago, said Keneshia Grant, a Great Migration expert at Howard University. For many, the question became, "should we go and try for a better life in these other places ... or should we stay and fight where we are?" Grant said.
  • "It was about economic opportunity, but I also think it was about terrorism too," Cassandra Overton Welchlin, executive director of the Mississippi Black Women's Roundtable, told Axios, pointing to the lynchings that drove families away.

Welchlin left Mississippi for graduate school and considered staying away.

  • "I did not want to come back to Mississippi because it is hard here," she told Axios.
  • Mentors encouraged her to return. She did, eventually becoming a voting rights organizer.

Zoom in: "What Colom did is he really jazzed up his base. He didn't run from them," King said. "His campaign style and that strategy can certainly serve as a model" for future campaigns.

  • Welchlin pointed to years of "nickeling and diming, doing organizing work to make sure that people had what they need to turn out the vote."

Between the lines: Colom rode a Democratic wave and discontent with the Trump administration's economic policies, but those conditions may be difficult to recreate, said Andra Gillespie, who studies Black voter behavior at Emory University.

  • Black residents make up roughly 37% of Mississippi's population, while most white voters favor Republicans. Unlike Georgia, Mississippi lacks the same diverse potential Democratic coalition.
  • "[T]he conditions that we see this year are probably not going to be the new normal," Gillespie says. "It'd be way too early to diagnose that there's a realignment happening."

Welchlin also cautioned that one historic victory doesn't mean Mississippi's racial barriers have disappeared.

  • "We understand here in Mississippi that racism ain't over, ... Racism is still very much embedded in everything from our policies to our elections."

What we're watching: Mississippi holds elections for governor, other statewide offices and state legislators in November 2027, testing whether Colom's coalition can hold.

  • "For the first time in forever, Mississippi Democrats will go into an election with momentum," King said.

The bottom line: Welchlin hopes Colom's victory changes how Black Mississippians view their futures: "I believe ... this election has given people hope that maybe I can stay here and be that change."

Go deeper: The Mississippi Delta helped carry Scott Colom to Senate history

item.title: Jensen Huang's implosion at Nvidia leaves trail of collateral damage
item.description:
Jensen Huang's self-destruction has left a trail of collateral damage that threatens to ensnare the board of Nvidia and the AI boom itself.

Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise.

The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap.

  • "His visionary leadership is going to be missed — it's not going to be replaced," Joel Shulman, CEO of ERShares, which has owned Nvidia shares since 2005, tells Axios.

Zoom in: With the uncertainty over Huang's tenure at Nvidia now resolved, the attention will quickly pivot to a slew of unanswered questions, including:

What will the investigations uncover?

  • Just because he's gone doesn't mean this is over. If the FBI probe or the independent investigation ordered by the board show that Huang gave favorable treatment to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy Alice Huang — he and Nvidia could face serious consequences.
  • Huang is also expected to testify behind closed doors next week before a Congressional committee.

Critics say the Nvidia board wasn't fulfilling its duty to provide proper oversight of Huang — particularly if it had any reason to be aware of his reported affairs before they become public.

  • Peter Jaworski, business ethics professor at Georgetown University, said the situation raises questions about what the board knew and when they knew it.
  • Nvidia reps haven't responded to Axios requests for comment on the board's handling of the matter.

Who takes the permanent role as CEO?

  • CFO Colette Kress was named to the interim role, but the board is conducting a global search that will consider outside and internal candidates for a permanant successor. She "has built enormous credibility internally and externally and we are big fans of her strategically," tech bull Dan Ives wrote Thursday in a research note.
  • Prediction markets point to Nvidia hyperscaling tech exec Ian Buck as the the leading candidate, but the political ramifications of Nvidia's position in the global economy may demand someone with more experience with geopolitics.
  • President Trump suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook, whom Ives also floated, but Kalshi traders rate that as a 1 in 25 shot.

Threat level: Could this be the catalyst that pops the AI bubble?

  • Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars — and Huang is at the center of that vast flywheel, Axios' Zachary Basu writes.

Next week becomes a "critical" moment with Tuesday's Nvidia earnings report and Thursday's likely Anthropic IPO, Shulman says.

  • "This Nvidia story is going to take a little air out of the balloon for the Anthropic IPO," he says.

The other side: Bret Greenstein, chief AI officer at consultancy West Monroe, argued that Huang's departure won't change the demand for chips:

  • "The company was never the source of AI demand. It has been supplying the capacity to meet that demand," which remains "enormous," he wrote today.

Follow the money: Will Huang's exit fundamentally reshape the long-term competitive landscape of the chip industry?

  • Competitors like AMD, Alphabet and Intel could benefit if chips customers are soured on working with Nvidia.
  • "When a star leaves a Wall Street firm, the first question is always the same: did the clients sign with the banker — or with the bank? Nvidia is about to answer that question on the biggest stage in the market," writes Mark Malek, CIO at Siebert Financial.

What's the floor for Nvidia's stock?

  • Nvidia shares were down another 5.7% just before 3pm Thursday and are now down 27% over the last month, having lost about $1 trillion in value.
  • "With this kind of leadership uncertainty, it's very difficult to predict where shares go over the next several trading sessions," writes Ken Mahoney, CEO of Mahoney Asset Management. "Sometimes huge news catalysts like this take all technicals out of the equation."

The intrigue: Will someone take a risk on hiring Huang?

  • Elon Musk has already hinted he could hire the former Nvidia chief as he moves toward a possible merger of SpaceX and Tesla.
  • But it'll be hard for anyone to hire Huang unless and until the FBI probe in particular is resolved.

The bottom line: The fallout is just beginning.

item.title: Zelensky says Musk-owned satellite system throttled again, Space X denies it
item.description:
The Ukrainian government has asked the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain new restrictions it says are disrupting the satellite system its military uses to intercept Russian drones.

Why it matters: This is the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine reported that Starshield, made by Elon Musk's SpaceX, was impeded.

  • The Ukrainian military uses Starshield — the military version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications system — to control and operate its reconnaissance and to intercept drones.

The other side: SpaceX respond Axios: "This is false. There has been no change."

Driving the news: Ukrainian President Zelensky said Thursday he was briefed by the minister of defense and the commander of the Ukrainian military that "units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations" along the entire front line and in the parts of Ukraine occupied by Russia.

  • "The Ukrainian military have already investigated the circumstances, and these are not random errors but systematic speed restrictions," he wrote on X. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side."

Zoom in: A Ukrainian official said the restrictions have been happening for three days.

  • "On the first day there were 10% limitations, on the second day 50%, and today 100% of the missions fail because of restrictions," the official said.
  • Ukraine's charge d'affaires to the U.S., Denys Sienik, said the Starshield system shuts down when drones fly at more than 100 miles per hour.
  • "We don't have clarification from SpaceX or Pentagon at the moment," he said.

State of play: Zelensky said the new restrictions began shortly before President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met at the Kremlin with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.

  • Kushner and Witkoff are expected to meet Zelensky later on Thursday in Dublin.

What they're saying: The bipartisan Congressional Ukraine Caucus said in a statement that it was "extremely alarmed" by the reports of a Starshield slowdown and "demanding a full accounting" from the Trump administration and SpaceX.

Catch up quick: Ukraine relies on two SpaceX satellite services. Starlink, the commercial service, supports battlefield communications and logistics.

  • Starshield is designed for government and military customers. Ukraine accesses it through a U.S. government agreement and uses it to operate reconnaissance drones and intercept Russian attack drones.
  • The Defense Department and SpaceX did not immediately return requests for comment.

item.title: Fed faces tougher inflation fight as pressure builds for more rate hikes
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it.

Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign.

  • But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight.
  • That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy.

What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday.

Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month.

  • Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs.
  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%.
  • Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June.

The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace.

  • The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May.
  • The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI, which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025.
  • More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X.

Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation.

  • Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates.
  • Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates.
  • Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning.

What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing.

  • President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border.
  • Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran, raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.
item.content:encoded:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation is no longer confined to a handful of trouble spots. Now, Federal Reserve officials are starting to question whether raising interest rates gradually will be enough to contain it.

Why it matters: Fed officials had hoped that a relatively modest series of interest rate hikes would be enough to bring inflation under control — more a recalibration than a tightening campaign.

  • But stubbornly high — and increasingly widespread — price pressures are raising the possibility of a more prolonged tightening campaign, with no clear endpoint in sight.
  • That would leave the Fed facing a more difficult balancing act: raising rates enough to contain inflation without unnecessarily damaging the economy.

What they're saying: "We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing — and we're going to have to deal with that," Chicago Fed president Austan Goolsbee, who called the inflation data "borderline disturbing," said late Tuesday.

Driving the news: Treasury yields are surging after Tuesday's hot inflation report and hawkish commentary from Fed officials — including governor Christopher Waller, who raised the prospect of a supersized rate hike next month.

  • Short-term yields have risen more sharply than longer-term yields, a sign that investors expect the Fed may need to raise rates more aggressively than previously anticipated.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note is still marching higher after surging 17 basis points on Tuesday, which was the biggest one-day surge since April 2025 — when markets were reeling from the "liberation day" tariffs.
  • The yield on the 10-year Treasury note jumped about 8 basis points, putting it back above 5%.
  • Financial markets see a December rate hike as virtually certain, according to CME FedWatch. Expectations for next year are trending higher, with traders now pricing in two additional quarter-point hikes by June.

The big picture: Measures designed to strip out unusually large price swings suggest that underlying inflation pressures are gaining pace.

  • The Cleveland Fed's trimmed-mean Consumer Price Index —which filters out unusually large price swings to give a clearer picture of underlying inflation — rose 0.4% in October, the largest monthly increase since May.
  • The Atlanta Fed's sticky-price CPI, which tracks prices that typically change, slowly accelerated to a 4.7% annualized pace in October, its fastest since February 2025.
  • More than three-quarters of the consumer price basket saw prices rise at an annualized rate exceeding 2% in October, the largest share since August 2022, Charles Schwab's head of macro research Kevin Gordon posted on X.

Yes, but: The Fed may have reason to proceed cautiously even against the backdrop of stubborn inflation.

  • Rising bond yields and a sell-off in technology stocks (revived again by the exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang) are already tightening financial conditions — potentially doing some of the work of higher interest rates.
  • Fed governor Michelle Bowman said in a speech that falling stock prices, higher borrowing costs and a stronger dollar could weigh on economic growth, particularly in sectors already struggling with high interest rates.
  • Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who dissented against the decision to hold rates steady last month, said she still supported a more gradual approach to raising rates. "It's less disruptive to the overall economy than moving in sharper, more aggressive movements," she said Thursday morning.

What to watch: Some of the forces driving inflation higher this year — including tariffs and the Iran war — were expected to be temporary. But the risk that they will prove more persistent keeps resurfacing.

  • President Trump threatened on Thursday morning to double tariffs on Mexican imports unless the nation stops a caravan of migrants from reaching the U.S. border.
  • Trump also said the U.S. doesn't need a deal with Iran, raising fresh questions about how soon the conflict (and the disruption to global energy supplies) might end.

item.title: Trump pitches Apple's Tim Cook as new Nvidia CEO
item.description:
President Trump is backing Apple executive chairman Tim Cook to replace tech giant Jensen Huang after Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO, though it's unclear whether he meant it as a joke.

The big picture: Trump didn't weigh in on the controversy surrounding Huang's departure following alleged affairs with a suspected Chinese spy and an Nvidia executive, instead calling Huang "a Legend" in his Truth Social post.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Trump sticks by Commerce Secretary Lutnick despite Nvidia inaction
item.description:
The White House is standing by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick despite a view within the administration that Lutnick delayed action to address concerns over chip smuggling to China.

Why it matters: Congress smells blood in the water following bombshell reports that U.S. national security may have been jeopardized by former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • Lawmakers want to know what the Trump administration did or did not do in response to that intelligence — and Lutnick, the official in charge of the department at the center of export control policy, is squarely in their field of view.

President Trump, however, is not distancing himself from the secretary.

  • "Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump's America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments," a White House official tells Axios.
  • "President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history."

Catch up quick: Lutnick was sent intelligence about Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy and repeatedly did not take export control action — despite pressure from the broader administration and the president himself, Axios first reported.

  • Lutnick's role is prompting scrutiny on the Hill from members on both sides of the aisle.
  • "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military," Senate Banking Committee Chair Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement.
  • "The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?," Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) told Politico.
  • "Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country," Kennedy added. "I mean, there will be a congressional investigation. But I don't think he ought to wait on Congress."

The Commerce Department has not confirmed for the record whether or not Lutnick has seen the memo.

Yes, but: "It's impossible that Howard Lutnick didn't know about this memo," one senior administration official told Axios.

  • "Of course Commerce got the memo. It had to get the memo. That's the point of the memo. It's about chips. Commerce deals with chips," a second official said.

Meanwhile, Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO following reports of a second affair with a direct report. He previously admitted to an affair and apologized, but members on both sides of the aisle are also not letting him off the hook.

  • "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Warren said.
  • Republican House Foreign Affairs Chair Brian Mast (Fla.) and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford (Ark.) told reporters on Thursday that Huang's resignation doesn't change their plans to probe him and the company, Bloomberg Government reported.
  • "Jensen Huang himself has been a pretty bold, some might even say arrogant promoter, sort of dismissing our concerns about China having access to these most advanced chips. And I do not take that lightly ... I would be happy to support a subpoena," Republican Sen. Kevin Cramer (N.D.) said on CNBC.

The bottom line: Resignations and apologies aside, Washington is ready to hold someone accountable as the FBI, Congress and Nvidia's board all investigate in tandem.

item.title: Jensen Huang, an architect of the AI boom, resigns as Nvidia CEO
item.description:
Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after he reportedly had two affairs, including one with a purported Chinese spy.

Why it matters: It's impossible to overstate how critical Huang is to Nvidia, to the AI buildout, to the stock market and economy.

  • His departure could, per Wall Street sources, be the catalyst that endangers a ballooning AI bubble.
  • It's also unlikely to ease congressional scrutiny of the company or Huang himself.

Driving the news: Nvidia's board named longtime CFO Colette Kress interim CEO, while launching a search for a permanent replacement.

  • Kress, who joined Nvidia in 2013, will continue serving as CFO while overseeing the company.
  • Harvey C. Jones was appointed Nvidia's first-ever board chair.
  • The board said it expects Nvidia's operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.

Zoom out: Huang's resignation follows revelations about two extramarital relationships.

  • The New York Times reported Wednesday that Huang had a relationship with Kimberly Powell, a senior Nvidia executive who reports to him.
  • Nvidia's board had previously launched an independent investigation into Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman identified by U.S. intelligence as a Chinese intelligence asset.
  • Nvidia did not provide a reason for Huang's resignation in Thursday's announcement, which comes after reports that the board had an emergency meeting over whether to oust the CEO.

By the numbers: Nvidia shares fell more than 10% after news of Huang's resignation.

  • One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang.

🚨 Stunning stat: At these levels, Nvidia will have lost about $1.4 trillion in market capitalization in two weeks, since the initial Times report about linking Jensen Huang and Alice Huang.

The big picture: This will likely go down as one of the biggest executive scandals in history.

  • Nvidia is also one of the largest holdings in major index funds because of its size, meaning this move has massive implications for every American with a retirement account.

The intrigue: Huang's resignation doesn't look like it'll ease congressional pressure over his behavior either.

  • "NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang's decision to resign does not absolve him, other executives, or the company as a whole of responsibility for putting our national security at risk or for any potential violations of our laws," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a statement.

The bottom line: The fallout is just starting.

This is breaking news.

item.title: Jensen Huang's ouster triggers an AI earthquake
item.description:
Jensen Huang's potential ouster from Nvidia has plunged the AI industry into uncharted territory — a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos unleashed by Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023.

Why it matters: Nvidia is the backbone of the global AI economy, with its chips, investments and financial guarantees sustaining an entire ecosystem of companies worth trillions of dollars.

  • At the center of that vast financial flywheel is Huang, who spent 33 years making himself synonymous with Nvidia — and Nvidia synonymous with the AI revolution.
  • "This is no ordinary CEO. This is no ordinary company. This is no ordinary sector. This is no ordinary time," economist Mohamed El-Erian wrote on X, warning of contagion across the AI industry.

Zoom in: As recently as two weeks ago, the notion of Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable.

  • Even after his affair with a suspected Chinese spy came to light, President Trump and Nvidia's board stood behind him, Silicon Valley's elite rallied to his defense and betting markets suggested he would survive.
  • It took revelations of a second affair — this time with an executive who reported directly to Huang — to shatter that consensus and bring his storied reign to the brink of a stunning end.

Driving the news: After that second affair came to light Wednesday night, Nvidia's board reportedly met to settle Huang's fate, though there was still no decision as of early Thursday morning. The White House was read in.

  • The market reaction has been brutal. Nvidia had already shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the initial scandal erupted, and shares plunged further in after-hours and pre-market trading overnight.
  • One of Wall Street's most prominent voices on tech, analyst Dan Ives, said Nvidia was worth 25% less without Huang.

Zoom out: Huang's rise was the stuff of Silicon Valley legend: The Taiwanese immigrant went from cleaning toilets at a Kentucky boarding school and waiting tables at Denny's to building one of the most valuable companies in history.

  • Huang and two fellow engineers hatched the idea for Nvidia at a Denny's booth in 1993, launching a chipmaker that would revolutionize gaming, transform modern computing and ultimately power the AI revolution.
  • Clad in his trademark black leather jacket, Huang became a global AI rock star — with a cult of personality that drew adoring crowds, calmed markets and commanded the attention of world leaders.

The big picture: Huang's apparent downfall comes amid mounting anxiety over the AI industry's future, as new financial, political and regulatory risks threaten one of the largest infrastructure buildouts in history.

  • The timing is especially fraught for Anthropic, whose historic IPO — backed by a $10 billion commitment from Nvidia — looms as a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade.
  • Huang spent years defending the industry's soaring valuations and dismissing warnings of a speculative frenzy. Now his own scandals could help burst the bubble he insisted didn't exist.

What to watch: The blast radius could extend far beyond Silicon Valley and Wall Street, threatening to engulf the Trump administration in a scandal over its handling of sensitive technology exports to China.

  • Huang forged a close alliance with Trump and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who loosened restrictions on chip sales even as other officials raised concerns about Chinese espionage and smuggling.
  • Top Senate Democrats are already demanding that Lutnick and other senior officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang, laying the groundwork for a sweeping investigation.

The bottom line: As veteran China watcher Bill Bishop wrote after Huang acknowledged his first affair: "There is rarely just one lie."

item.title: Trump orders Vance to focus on "corruption" in Democrat-run areas, not Iran
item.description:
President Trump directed Vice President JD Vance on Thursday to turn his "complete and total attention" toward alleged corruption in Democrat-run cities and states, contending that "[w]e don't need a deal with Iran."

The big picture: After Vance concluded that the Iran war drove Republicans' stunning midterm walloping, Trump is reorienting his No. 2's focus — and directing him to go after Democrats the president labeled as "CORRUPT AND EVIL."

  • Oil prices surged, and stocks sank after Trump's post reinjected a note of uncertainty into a market that was acting like the Iran war was all but over.

Driving the news: "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • Also on Truth Social Thursday, he threatened new tariffs on Mexico and criticized GOP senators for failing to pass the Save America ACT — adding that failure to do so was "devastating" for Republicans during the midterms.
  • He said that he had asked Vance to "focus his complete and total attention" on so-called "Corruption and Crime" in Democrat-run cities and states, naming Minnesota, California and Illinois.

Vance has chaired Trump's Task Force to Eliminate Fraud since the president created it via executive order earlier this year.

  • Throughout the first half of his administration and federal crackdown on U.S. cities, Trump has repeatedly framed blue areas as hotbeds of crime and corruption, even when the stats haven't necessarily backed up those arguments.

Catch up quick: Vance was recently heavily involved in a push to reach a new ceasefire with Iran and resume nuclear negotiations, Axios' Barak Ravid reported.

  • Vance was a skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war, Ravid reported, and led U.S. negotiating delegations after it began.
  • Vance's office and the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Between the lines: Vance offered a surprisingly candid assessment of the midterm shellacking, writing in an X post last week that "[t]he reason we lost is the war."

  • He continued: "If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest."
  • "But everyone knows why we lost."

What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, where he said Trump had considered resuming the war or cutting a deal but instead settled on strangling the Iranian regime, Axios previously reported.

  • Rubio has signaled skepticism of a diplomatic breakthrough — and Trump's post indicates that door is closed, for now.

Go deeper: Trump: New Iran attacks "quite unlikely"

item.title: Bracing for Nvidia's impact
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create.

Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia.

  • Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy.

Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

  • The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang.
  • Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session.

Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years.

  • The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers.
  • Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth.
  • There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle.
  • "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness."

Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session.

Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios.

  • With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100.

Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is.

  • It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman.
  • It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power.
  • That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds.
  • For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI.

Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers.

  • In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day.

State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement.

  • On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research.
  • "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
  • Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month.

What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis.

  • "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions."

The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history.

  • From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet.
  • He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993.

The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's apparent from grace is a shock to a company at the core of the U.S. markets and the AI ecosystem that he did much to create.

Why it matters: CEO scandals happen at companies. Their stocks fall. But there is no other company quite like Nvidia.

  • Its size, financial resources and strategic position in the AI boom have made both the chipmaker and Huang, personally, pillars of the industry that has come to drive both the stock market and the economy.

Catch up quick: Following revelations this week that Huang had admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman believed by the U.S. government to be a Chinese intelligence asset, the New York Times reported Wednesday evening that Huang also had a romantic relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

  • The Wall Street Journal and other outlets are reporting that the company's board of directors was preparing to oust Huang.
  • Nvidia shares plunged in the after-hours trading session.

Context: The uncertainty surrounding Huang's position comes as the AI trade is going through one of the crises of investor confidence that have periodically hammered AI shares in recent years.

  • The concern this time centers on the ability of the AI build-out to continue, as rising interest rates and a saturated market curtail the sale of bonds to pay for data centers.
  • Chip makers like Nvidia have been particularly hard hit by this recent AI slump. Its shares were down roughly 30% from their recent high through Wednesday's close, vaporizing nearly $1.59 trillion in shareholder wealth.
  • There have been market drawdowns around AI before, says Eric Sheridan, a research analyst at Goldman Sachs, in a big new report on the investment cycle.
  • "The stakes are undoubtedly higher now as we're further along in the cycle and the dollars being spent have grown considerably, which may be adding to investor skittishness."

Stunning stat: Since the end of last week, the company lost over $600 billion in market value through Wednesday's after market session.

Zoom out: Those losses will touch a lot of portfolios.

  • With a market capitalization of roughly $4.18 trillion — through Wednesday's close — Nvidia is the world's second-largest publicly traded company, behind Apple, giving it significant sway in market capitalization-weighted indexes, such as the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq 100.

Yes, but: If anything, a focus on Nvidia's massive size obscures how important the company is.

  • It dominates the market for the graphics processing units, or GPUs, that are the costliest input into AI data centers — about 75% of a data center's total cost, per Goldman.
  • It also finances and backstops significant chunks of AI computing power.
  • That means Nvidia is bankrolling a small army of AI firms: AI coding companies, data center operators, neoclouds.
  • For example: Nvidia has put more than $2 billion into CoreWeave, the troubled neocloud that's seen its borrowing costs soar in recent weeks. It has equity stakes in Anthropic and OpenAI.

Follow the money: Such was Nvidia's — and Huang's — stature in the tech world that in recent years, the mere mention of a company by the Nvidia CEO could create big market winners and losers.

  • In June, for example, positive comments from Huang about Marvell Technology sent the company's stock soaring nearly 33% in a single day.

State of play: Now, it's Nvidia shares that might need words of encouragement.

  • On Wednesday the stock received a downgrade to "market perform" from "outperform" from Bernstein Research.
  • "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip," Bernstein's analysts wrote. "But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines."
  • Morgan Stanley also removed the company from its list of "top picks" earlier in the day, after the stock had declined more than 25% since it was named top pick last month.

What's next: Whatever comes next for Nvidia, the company is likely to be in an extended period of strategic paralysis.

  • "Decisions about acquisitions or investments or product roadmaps, those are the kinds of things that will now have to be paused, if — again — if this happens, all these things are going to have to pause," Gil Luria, an analyst covering Nvidia for the brokerage firm D.A. Davidson, tells Axios. "So it just slows the company down when it can't make the most important, biggest decisions."

The big picture: Huang has presided over one of the most remarkable explosions of wealth creation in market history.

  • From the closing price on its first day of trading, Nvidia's total compound return with dividend reinvestment is 462,906%, according to FactSet.
  • He has been at the helm of the company since he co-founded it in 1993.

The bottom line: But depending on how the situation plays out, shareholders may be about to find out what an Nvidia without its charismatic leader looks like.

item.title: From Emmett Till to Robert Johnson, the Delta powered Scott Colom's historic Senate bid
item.description:
Scott Colom's path to a historic U.S. Senate upset ran through the Mississippi Delta — where Emmett Till was abducted, Fannie Lou Hamer fought for the ballot and the blues became an American art form.

Why it matters: Nearly 150 years after Reconstruction, Mississippi sent a Black American to the U.S. Senate for the first time since 1881. The votes pushing Colom toward that milestone came from communities where Black residents spent generations fighting for the ballot.

Driving the news: The Associated Press projected the race for Colom on Wednesday, handing Democrats a historic upset over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.

By the numbers: An Axios analysis of AP county returns found Colom ahead in 16 of the 18 counties in the Mississippi Delta National Heritage Area.

  • Colom collected roughly 100,000 votes to Hyde-Smith's 62,000 — a 38,000-vote advantage.
  • In 2020, Democrat Mike Espy carried 15 of those counties by about 25,000 votes, according to Mississippi's certified county returns. Colom's share of the two-party vote climbed from about 56% to 62%.
  • Statewide, Colom led Hyde-Smith by about 4,700 votes out of more than 962,000 counted when the AP called the race Wednesday — a margin of roughly half a percentage point.

What they're saying: "Mississippi voters made history because they refused to be intimidated, discouraged, or counted out," NAACP president Derrick Johnson said in a statement.

  • Johnson said Mississippi voters showed up despite efforts to remove voters from the rolls.

Zoom in: Colom's electoral map traces some of the most painful and defining chapters of Black American history.

  • Coahoma County: Home to Clarksdale and the famed crossroads associated with the legend that bluesman Robert Johnson sold his soul to the devil. Colom led with about 4,700 votes to 1,300.
  • Leflore and Tallahatchie counties: Emmett Till was abducted near Money in Leflore County in 1955. His body was recovered from the Tallahatchie River in Tallahatchie County, where an all-white jury acquitted his killers. Colom led by about 4,200 votes in Leflore and 1,300 in Tallahatchie, according to AP returns.
  • Sunflower County: Fannie Lou Hamer, who lived in Ruleville, challenged Mississippi's racist voting restrictions. As late as the spring of 1965, only 155 Black residents had registered to vote in the county, according to the Mississippi Department of Archives and History. Colom led with about 5,300 votes to 1,700.
  • Washington County: Robert F. Kennedy visited Greenville during his 1967 tour of Delta poverty. 29.4% of Washington County is still in poverty per the Census Bureau's 2020–2024 estimate. Colom led with about 8,700 votes to 2,400.

Zoom out: Colom didn't suddenly turn the Delta blue. Espy won most of it in 2020. But Colom widened the Democratic margin.

  • In DeSoto County, which falls within the heritage area but outside the Delta's historic heartland, Colom led by about 3,300 votes. Hyde-Smith won there by roughly 12,100 in 2020.
  • Colom also swept the Golden Triangle counties of Lowndes, Oktibbeha and Clay, his home region in northeastern Mississippi. He won all three by double-digit margins and improved on Espy's 2020 performance.

Between the lines: The historical symbolism stretches beyond the Delta.

  • Colom led with about 12,100 votes to 9,700 in Forrest County, named for Confederate Gen. Nathan Bedford Forrest, the Ku Klux Klan's first grand wizard.
  • Hyde-Smith faced criticism during her 2018 race against Espy after saying she would sit in the front row if invited to a public hanging. She later apologized to those offended.

The bottom line: The region where Black Mississippians fought some of America's fiercest battles for voting rights helped elect the state's first Black U.S. senator in 145 years — and raised a new question.

  • Can political representation finally bring economic change to the Delta?

item.title: Democrats debate taking a page from Trump's economic playbook
item.description:
President Trump is turning the federal government into an investor in dozens of private companies, and some Democrats are considering following his lead as their party emerges emboldened from the midterm elections.

Why it matters: Democrats are gaining new power to scrutinize Trump's corporate investments, even as his approach gains traction within their own party.

  • They're looking at investments and aid for clean energy and other priorities, like support for energy infrastructure.

State of play: The Trump administration's investments in energy, critical minerals and other industries are already drawing calls for congressional investigations.

"The Trump administration has widened the aperture for industrial policy," Jennifer Granholm, who served as President Biden's Energy Secretary, said at a gathering of energy and climate experts Axios attended in Berkeley, Calif., last month.

  • "You're not going to have state ownership of enterprises," Granholm told Axios in an interview afterward. "But maybe you do take a little bit of an ownership slice" for national security or global competitiveness reasons, she said.
  • Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has also expressed openness to federal ownership stakes, while raising concerns about the Trump administration's lack of transparency and accountability, he told Semafor.

Rep. Sean Casten (D-Ill.) has argued that the U.S. needs to consider a more aggressive industrial policy to compete with countries like China, while warning against direct government ownership.

  • "We are long overdue for having a conversation about, 'should the United States even have an industrial policy?'" Casten said at a recent University of Chicago event. "For a long time, we viewed industrial policy as something that socialists do."
  • Casten said he would support the U.S. ensuring domestic manufacturing of certain parts of supply chains, like electronic control systems that operate energy infrastructure, and even pursuing "smart tariff policy" to have competitive markets.

The big picture: The Biden administration spent billions subsidizing clean energy and semiconductor manufacturing. Trump has taken government intervention a step further by acquiring ownership stakes in companies ranging from Intel to critical mineral producers.

  • It's been a striking reversal for a president who has repeatedly criticized Democrats for government overreach.

How it works: The Trump administration has announced more than $30 billion in investments across nearly 50 deals involving government ownership and related financial arrangements, according to a Council on Foreign Relations tracker.

  • The investments span semiconductors, critical minerals and energy — strategically important industries where high costs and long development timelines can make private financing difficult.

Flashback: Washington has taken ownership stakes in private companies before, including during the 2008 financial crisis. But those investments were intended as temporary measures to rescue struggling businesses, unlike Trump's national security-focused investments.

What they're saying: "Equity from the U.S. government can act as patient capital that helps derisk an investment with a long time horizon or technological risk that would otherwise not attract sufficient private investment," said Jonathan Hillman, a Council on Foreign Relations fellow behind the tracker.

  • Hillman said the deals announced since January 2025 have also mobilized $28.5 billion in private capital.

Yes, but: Some politicians and energy leaders warn that direct government ownership could open the door to political favoritism and market distortions.

  • "Government is not a venture capital fund. It's not a private equity fund. It's not well suited to pick winners and losers in the marketplace," said Tim Pawlenty, former Republican governor of Minnesota who now leads the Solar Energy Industries Association, at the same University of Chicago event.
  • "If it starts to go down the slippery slope of 'it's just the flavor of the day company because we like it' or they're well connected or whatever, then you got problems."

Threat level: "Buying stakes in public companies is so, so, so dangerous," Casten said.

  • "I have no idea how a future president unwinds our stake in Intel without totally tanking Intel stock," he added, referring to the administration's roughly 10% stake in the semiconductor giant.
  • To avoid such concerns, Hillman suggests creating a federal chief investment officer to oversee investments and eventual sales.

The other side: The White House defended the investments as a way to rebuild American manufacturing and secure critical supply chains, emphasizing that companies participate voluntarily, spokesman Matthew Middleton said.

What we're watching: Democrats could spend the next two years scrutinizing Trump's investments — while debating whether a future Democratic administration should make similar deals of its own.

item.title: Democrats unite against Big Health Care
item.description:
Newly elected Democrats from ruby red states are leading a charge to take on corporate health care and some business practices that they say drive up health care costs.

Why it matters: Democrats may not be anywhere close to agreement on Medicare for All, but they're relatively united around confronting Big Health Care after campaigning hard on the populist theme.

Driving the news: While expanding Medicare, reversing GOP Medicaid cuts and reviving enhanced Obamacare subsidies are getting most of the attention, there's a subtle shift in rhetoric and policy positions toward blaming big health companies for the affordability crisis.

  • It reflects the reality that a substantial expansion of the federal government's role in health care isn't in the cards while President Trump is in office, but populist themes could unite the rank-and-file and even draw in some Republicans.
  • Even candidates who didn't constantly rail about drugmakers or insurers have adopted policy ideas that, until recently, were confined to left-leaning think tanks.

Case in point: Incoming Texas Sen. James Talarico ran on breaking up big health care companies and "stop[ping] hospitals and insurance companies from overcharging patients." (He also supports allowing Americans under 65 to join Medicare.)

  • South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews ran on limiting insurer profits per enrollee, expanding the number of drugs subject to Medicare drug price negotiations and banning private equity-owned hospitals.
  • Incoming Kansas Sen. Adam Hamilton supports expanding Medicare drug price negotiations and extending the negotiated prices to private health plans, as well as addressing Medicare Advantage overpayments from the federal government.
  • Other targets include medical debt, pharmacy benefit manager practices and caps on out-of-pocket drug costs.

Many of these ideas already have buy-in from more-senior progressives.

  • Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) has sponsored the Break Up Big Medicine Act, which is co-sponsored by Republican Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, which would prohibit common ownership of health plans and providers.
  • Incoming Michigan Sen. Abdul El-Sayed, an avid Medicare for All supporter, ran on support of the Warren-Hawley bill, as well as expanding Medicare drug price negotiations.
  • The House's health care working group, made up of both progressives and moderates, pitched capping "excessive" hospital prices and enacting site-neutral payments.

The big picture: Voters have made clear that they want lower health care costs. So while a broad overhaul of the health system may not immediately be on the table, Democrats are looking for ways to deliver.

  • Powerful health industry groups are poised to push back, arguing that the populist policies would threaten patient care and access in some communities.
  • But the ideas under discussion could gain favor with some Republicans.

What they're saying: When asked at an Axios event on Tuesday whether Congress should address ownership ties between insurers, PBMs and pharmacies, Rep. Morgan Griffith — the top Republican on the House Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — said, "I've only heard the case for breaking them up."

  • "There's just something in your gut that bothers you when your pharmacy, your PBM and your insurance company are all owned by the same people," he added.

What we're watching: Forcing drugmakers to lower prescription drug prices could be a particularly compelling target, given Trump's demonstrated interest in the topic.

  • He has previously called on Congress to codify the "most-favored-nation" deals he made with pharmaceutical manufacturers that require the companies, in some cases, to offer Americans prices on a par with what's paid abroad.
  • The Senate Finance Committee's top Democrat, Ron Wyden of Oregon, told reporters this week that he's open to a deal codifying those agreements in exchange for an expansion of the number of drugs Medicare can negotiate on, according to InsideHealthPolicy.

The bottom line: It was only four years ago that Democrats struggled to find enough votes for the modest drug price negotiations that exist today, marking the first successful legislative attempt to directly lower health care costs in any sector by either party.

  • Now, they're more willing to push for change and confront big industry players.
