item.title: Scoop: AOC shakes up team again as 2028 decision looms
item.description:
New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life.

Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year.

Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision.

  • At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns.
  • Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period.
  • AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers.

But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid.

  • Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House.
  • It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website.
  • Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign.

Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported.

  • They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides.
  • The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide.

What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment.

  • Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.
item.content:encoded:
New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez is shaking up her team for the second time in the past few months as she prepares to make the biggest decision of her political life.

Why it matters: The overhaul comes as the democratic socialist leader is debating whether to run for president in 2028 — or Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer's seat, which is up the same year.

Zoom in: Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with her longtime digital fundraising firm, Middle Seat, according to three people familiar with the decision.

  • At the same time, sources said, she's brought on Aisle 518 Strategies — the company led by Democratic strategist Tim Tagaris, who oversaw Bernie Sanders' record-breaking online fundraising strategy in his two presidential campaigns.
  • Middle Seat has been key to Ocasio-Cortez's operation. Over the past two years, she has paid the firm more than $6 million — about a quarter of her operation's disbursements during that period.
  • AOC is close with Sanders, and if she decides to run for president, progressives say, she would be able to quickly staff up with his former advisers.

But Ocasio-Cortez's latest move doesn't necessarily signal that she's leaning toward a presidential run or a Senate bid.

  • Tagaris' firm has helped power the small-dollar fundraising operation for California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who's widely expected to run for the White House.
  • It also has worked with other Democrats who are potential contenders for president — Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff and former Vice President Kamala Harris, according to the company's website.
  • Middle Seat, the firm AOC is leaving, has Sanders roots as well: It was founded by alumni of the Vermont senator's 2016 campaign.

Flashback: Ocasio-Cortez's reorganizing follows several changes she made to her staff this year, as Axios previously reported.

  • They included parting ways with her longtime campaign manager and creative director, as well as bringing aboard a few former aides.
  • The Washington Sun reported this week that AOC had hired Freeland Ellis, a Sanders alum, as a communications aide.

What they're saying: A spokesperson for Ocasio-Cortez declined to comment.

  • Tagaris declined to comment, and Middle Seat partner Kenneth Pennington did not respond to a request for comment.
item.dc:creator: Holly Otterbein
Alex Thompson

item.title: How the midterms swing each party's economic feelings
item.description:
Note: Figures compare average daily sentiment readings over the seven days before each election with the five days after. Election Day is excluded; Data: Morning Consult; Chart: Emily Peck/Axios

There was an unusually sharp partisan mood shift in the wake of the midterms, according to sentiment data from Morning Consult that was shared exclusively with Axios.

Why it matters: While big partisan swings in consumer sentiment are typical after a presidential election, they have been much smaller in midterm races.

  • The latest numbers show just how tightly Americans' views on the economy are now intertwined with politics.

By the numbers: Democratic consumer sentiment rose 6.5 points in the five days after the election compared with the week before, while Republicans' mood fell 6.4 points.

How it works: Morning Consult's index considers survey responses from approximately 5,000 U.S. adults.

  • They're asked five questions, including on people's personal finances and financial outlook, as well as their views on overall business conditions.

Zoom in: The biggest shifts in sentiment were in respondents' feelings about the future.

  • Republicans' outlook across all five metrics fell after the election. Their confidence in business conditions over the next five years plummeted 12 percentage points.
  • Democrats, meanwhile, had a jump of 9 percentage points in confidence about business conditions (although they remain negative about it) and an even bigger increase — 12 percentage points — in optimism that their own finances would improve over the next year.
  • Of note: Both sides were more negative about their own finances compared with a year ago.

Zoom out: Overall sentiment, which includes Independents, barely moved — ticking up less than one point, per Morning Consult. The opposing partisan shifts appear to have canceled each other out.

Reality check: It's early days, and sentiment could shift quickly.

Between the lines: Consumer sentiment was once a telling measure of how people would actually spend their money: Good vibes meant more spending.

  • Lately, it's looked more like a political measure.
  • "Sentiment matters because it's vibes," says Eli Yokley, a U.S. politics analyst at Morning Consult.

item.title: Murders plunge 17% in America's biggest cities
item.description:
Data: Major Cities Chiefs Association (MCCA); Note: Tulsa Police changed crime-reporting systems, which may affect year-over-year comparisons.; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios

Homicides fell 15.2% across major U.S. police jurisdictions through the first nine months of 2026, extending a retreat from pandemic-era violence that began under President Biden and continues under President Trump.

The big picture: A new Major Cities Chiefs Association report found declines in all four major violent-crime categories among 66 reporting U.S. large law enforcement agencies from January through September, compared with the same period last year.

  • Homicides dropped 15.2%.
  • Robberies fell 9.1%.
  • Rapes declined 3.5%.
  • Aggravated assaults decreased 3.4%.

State of play: Combined, the four categories fell 4.9% — or 13,822 fewer reported offenses.

  • Fifty-one of the 66 agencies reported overall declines.
  • Homicides dropped in 49 jurisdictions, increased in 15 and remained unchanged in two.

Zoom in: Some of the nation's largest cities recorded striking homicide declines.

  • Memphis: Homicides plunged 36.5%, from 156 to 99.
  • San Antonio was down 36.5%, Indianapolis down 33.6%, Philadelphia down 21.2%, Aurora, Colorado down 65.2% and Newark, New Jersey down 59.1%.

The other side: New York City was a major outlier and reported more violent crime in all four categories, including 24.5% more homicides and 14.2% more robberies. Its combined violent crime total was up 5.1%.

  • San Diego reported 45.2% more homicides and Las Vegas recorded a 23.4% jump.
  • Washington, D.C., saw homicides fall 29.9%, but robberies surged 41.1%, pushing its combined violent-crime total up 9.7%.

The caveat: The figures remain preliminary. Houston reported no data because of a records-system transition, and Tulsa recently transitioned to a new crime reporting system, the report notes.

item.title: Outgoing Trump foe Massie forces new Epstein files showdown
item.description:
Outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) secured the 218 signatures needed to force another House showdown over the Jeffrey Epstein files Wednesday, just one day after fellow Republicans blocked his attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Why it matters: Congress overwhelmingly voted last year to force the release of the Epstein files, but survivors and lawmakers say the Trump administration has still withheld records. The new bill would give them the power to sue the DOJ and help state prosecutors pursue investigations.

Driving the news: Massie announced Wednesday afternoon that his discharge petition for the Epstein Files Transparency Act II had reached the required 218 signatures.

  • Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.) provided the final signature Wednesday, according to the House clerk's records.
  • Just four Republicans signed the petition: Massie, Nancy Mace of South Carolina, Ralph Norman of South Carolina and Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania. The other 214 signatures came from Democrats.

What he's saying: "I'm working closely with @RepJayapal, @RepTeresaLF and @RepRoKhanna to get this to the floor for a vote soon," Massie wrote on X.

The other side: The White House didn't answer questions about the bill.

  • In a statement, spokesperson Lauren Bis said President Trump has "been totally exonerated on anything relating to Epstein. And by releasing thousands of pages of documents, cooperating with the House Oversight Committee's subpoena request, signing the Epstein Files Transparency Act, and calling for more investigations into Epstein's Democrat friends, President Trump has done more for Epstein's victims than anyone before him."
  • Speaker Mike Johnson's office did not respond to a request for comment.

The intrigue: President Trump helped drive Massie out of Congress by backing a primary challenger, but the Kentucky Republican is using his final weeks in office to challenge the administration on some of its most politically sensitive topics.

  • This latest effort could force Republicans to revisit a scandal that dogged the Trump administration for more than a year, even after Congress overwhelmingly voted to require the release of Epstein's files.
  • This time, Massie wants to give Epstein survivors, state prosecutors and lawmakers the power to sue the Justice Department over records they believe it has unlawfully withheld.

Catch up quick: Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) led the original push to force the release of the Epstein files.

  • Their first bill passed the House 427-1 in November 2025 after they secured enough signatures to bypass Speaker Mike Johnson. Trump ultimately signed it into law.
  • The law required DOJ to release its Epstein-related investigative records by Dec. 19, 2025, with limited exceptions to protect victims, ongoing investigations and other sensitive information.
  • The department missed that deadline but announced in January that it had released nearly 3.5 million pages.

The controversy: Epstein survivors and lawmakers have accused DOJ of withholding too much information while simultaneously exposing victims through inadequate redactions.

  • A report released Tuesday by the Republican-led House Oversight Committee faulted the Trump administration's handling of the disclosures, including failures to protect victims and excessive redactions concealing alleged co-conspirators.
  • The committee also said its investigation found no evidence implicating Trump in Epstein's crimes.

What's next: Massie's petition is expected to become eligible for a floor vote by early December, with more than enough legislative days remaining under the House's current schedule.

  • But passage is not guaranteed, and Senate Republican leaders could still decline to consider the measure before the new Congress takes office in January.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to add the White House's comment.

item.title: Scott Colom ousts Cindy Hyde-Smith in historic Mississippi Senate flip
item.description:
Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in a stunning Mississippi upset, becoming the first Democrat elected to the state's Senate delegation since 1982, AP projects.

Why it matters: Colom's victory marks another extraordinary breakthrough for Democrats in the Deep South, extending the historic blue wave that handed the party control of both chambers of Congress.

  • Colom also becomes Mississippi's first Black senator since Reconstruction.
  • Hiram Rhodes Revels became the nation's first Black senator in 1870. Mississippi's last Black senator, Blanche K. Bruce, served until 1881.

Catch up quick: Colom's victory expands Democrats' 55–44 advantage over Republicans in the Senate.

  • Worries of a recount — which requires a court order, as Mississippi has no recount law — seemed moot as Hyde-Smith posted a video message to X shortly after AP called the race, appearing to concede to Colom.
  • "While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters. I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state," she said.
  • Hyde-Smith also addressed another worry from Mississippi voters following a significant purge of the state's voter rolls, saying that her campaign "has worked tirelessly to ensure every legally cast vote was counted and that the people of Mississippi received a fair and transparent election."
  • "I am proud of what we have accomplished together, but I want to make one thing very clear: an election may come to an end, but our commitment to Mississippi never will," she said.

The big picture: Colom's victory followed a late surge of Democratic spending and organizing in a state Trump carried by 23 points in 2024.

  • Hyde-Smith faced warning signs in the campaign's closing months, when Colom raised twice as much as the GOP senator despite her overall cash advantage.
  • She was also outspent on TV advertising, with a flood of ads from left-leaning PACs and super PACs pushing support for Colom and attacking the senator for her vote not to release files related to the convicted human trafficker Jeffrey Epstein.
  • Hyde-Smith's campaign also faced criticism over an interview she gave to WLOX-TV in Biloxi, Mississippi, where she fumbled an answer about the price of beef, saying that Mississippians had "so many other proteins to choose from."
  • Colom's campaign capitalized on her blunder, creating a viral campaign ad urging voters to "choose another senator."

The GOP made a late push to help Hyde-Smith, including President Trump speaking at a rally for her in Alcorn County, where he won by 68% in 2024.

  • But it wasn't enough. Hyde-Smith's term will end after eight years.
  • She was appointed to the Senate in 2018 by then-Mississippi Gov. Phil Bryant, and ran for a full term in 2020, where she bested her Democratic challenger Mike Espy by 10 points.

Zoom in: Colom, a 43-year-old district attorney from Columbus, campaigned on lowering the cost of living, raising wages and protecting rural hospitals.

  • His campaign also drew in heavy Democratic hitters to stump for him, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock.

The bottom line: Colom's win adds Mississippi to a growing list of Republican strongholds where Democrats broke through in the midterms, including Texas and South Carolina.

  • It also reinforces the role of Black voters in the Democratic comeback, after the party rebuilt support among a crucial voting bloc that showed signs of shifting toward Trump in 2024.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

This story has been corrected to show that Hyde-Smith's interview was conducted in Biloxi (not Jackson, Mississippi).

item.title: Scoop: Lutnick stalled curbing Nvidia chip sales to China — again — after Oval Office showdown
item.description:
President Trump on Thursday authorized a crack down on companies suspected of diverting Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China for the third time this year — even consulting Elon Musk before giving the go-ahead.

  • One administration official has repeatedly stood in the way: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Why it matters: This standoff illustrates a breakdown in efforts to keep American technology out of China's hands as the world wonders why the Trump administration has not taken action against the company at the center of suspected chip smuggling — and an espionage scandal.

  • This report was assembled from interviews with six high-level sources who were briefed on or, in some cases, heard the discussions.

Inside the room: On Thursday, as the spy scandal rocked the administration, Lutnick met in the Situation Room with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

  • During the meeting, Bessent confronted Lutnick about why his department has resisted implementing the export controls, particularly on Megaspeed, the company at the center of the spy scandal. The group sided with Bessent.
  • Lutnick appeared to agree, but then muttered under his breath, "I need to check with the president."

Friction point: Lutnick's seemingly innocuous comment raised concerns, the sources said, because officials have repeatedly believed the Commerce Department would impose the export controls, only to have nothing happen.

  • "He's stalling it out," said one official, describing how Lutnick had previously met privately with the president to change his mind about the export limit.
  • "This is an ongoing concern with Howard and this issue," said another.

This time, one person in the room called his bluff by saying: "Great. Why don't we do it today?"

  • Around 5pm, the group headed to the Oval Office.
  • Trump called tech advisor Elon Musk and agreed to move forward. Musk supported Rubio, Bessent, Greer and Hegseth's case to impose the controls while Lutnick warned it "will start a trade war with China."
  • "Everyone argued back that China is already doing to us what Lutnick warned would happen," a source said.

Behind the scenes: With Lutnick the lone holdout, Trump made his decision: "Let's get it done." But once everyone was outside of the Oval Office, Lutnick proposed a new delay tactic.

  • "I'll develop some options and come back," he said.
  • "Everyone was like: 'No, no, the decision's been made. Go fucking execute,'" one source said. "Well, it still hasn't happened."

The other side: Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer denied that Bessent confronted Lutnick and would not immediately comment on the other allegations.

Flashback: On at least three separate occasions — in May, August, and Nov. 5 — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China.

  • But Lutnick and Commerce Undersecretary Jeffrey Kessler resisted pressure from Bessent and others to move forward.
  • In May, a highly classified memo warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, a Megaspeed employee suspected by U.S. intelligence of being a Chinese agent, was shared with the president and other officials.
  • In a subsequent meeting, Bessent, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Hegseth and White House officials pressed Lutnick and Kessler to act, the source said, "and they were refusing."

Catch up quick: The Trump administration last year announced it would loosen export controls on Nvidia H200 chip sales to China — something Nvidia has lobbied hard for.

  • Trump has taken a more lax approach to export controls on China, agreeing to allow sales of Nvidia's H200 chips, which are older but still powerful, in exchange for a 25% tariff.
  • Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market.
  • The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S.

The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

  • Long before the affair with Alice Huang, Jensen Huang has pushed for tapping into the Chinese market.
  • The CEO at the center of an AI boom Trump is dead set on winning has largely been successful at convincing Trump and Lutnick that selling less powerful chips to China is good for national security because it prevents China from developing its own alternatives and keeps the adversary dependent on the U.S.

The bottom line: While Lutnick oversees the department squarely at the center of export control policy, Trump is the ultimate decider.

item.title: Scoop: U.S. asks Russia to propose new security agreement with Europe
item.description:
The U.S. has asked Russia to submit a new proposal for a future security agreement with Europe that includes Russian steps to ease tension with the continent, two sources with knowledge of the matter said.

Why it matters: For years, Russia has sought a European security deal that limits NATO expansion and scales back its military presence in Eastern Europe. The U.S. has rejected those demands in the past, but now appears open to them in some form as part of a broader agreement to end the war in Ukraine.

  • But many European governments are deeply suspicious of the administration's approach.

State of play: President Trump's envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff will meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday to reiterate the request. They also want Putin to allow European representatives to join the next round of Russia-Ukraine peace talks, a U.S. official said.

  • From Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff are expected to travel to Dublin to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Thursday night.

Catch up quick: The talks on Tuesday and Wednesday were the first time Ukrainian and Russian officials met with U.S. mediators present since February, when they were suspended due to the war in Iran.

  • In recent weeks, Witkoff and Kushner met with both Putin and Zelensky, creating a bit of momentum.
  • Putin agreed to resume peace talks and release U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard, who was detained by Russia in 2022. Together with first lady Melania Trump and her team, Witkoff and Kushner also brokered a humanitarian ceasefire in the city of Oleshky.

Driving the news: The talks in Abu Dhabi started on Tuesday with Witkoff, Kushner and commander of the U.S. European Command Gen. Alexus Grynkewich mediating between the Russians and the Ukrainians.

  • The parties agreed to a prisoner exchange deal that Kushner and Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said could be the biggest since the war began.
  • U.S. and Ukrainian officials said the exact number of prisoners to be released will be decided during meetings with Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.
  • Before and after the talks, the U.S. and Ukrainian negotiating teams briefed a delegation of senior diplomats from Germany, the U.K., France, Italy, the EU and NATO.

Behind the scenes: The meetings between the Russians and the Ukrainians on Tuesday were tense and at times emotional, with both sides airing grievances after nine months of not talking directly, according to a source in the room.

  • Kushner and Witkoff tried to lower the temperature, telling Russian and Ukrainian negotiators that the goal is to end this round of talks with options for the leaders on both sides.
  • Eventually, after each party made its case, the discussion became more constructive, the source said.
  • "We had pretty tough discussions," Kushner said at a press conference after the talks concluded on Wednesday.
  • "The Russians came with strict directives. It was very hard to soften it, but it ended productively," Arakhamia said.

Zoom in: The U.S. proposal to secure a deal on a new Europe-Russia security architecture as part of an agreement to end the war in Ukraine was a key focus of the Abu Dhabi talks.

  • Russian negotiators said Putin launched the invasion of Ukraine because then-President Biden did not reply to his 2021 letter laying out his security concerns, two sources with knowledge of the talks said.
  • According to one of the sources, Kushner and Witkoff told the Russians that the world has changed a lot since 2021.
  • They proposed that Russia draft a new proposal that includes its security concerns and demands, but also lays out what "symmetrical steps" it's willing to take to de-escalate and reassure Europe that it will not attack in the future.
  • Kushner and Witkoff also told the Russians that in order to seriously discuss security issues in Europe, they need to agree to allow European representatives to participate in future peace talks.
  • "We told the Russians, they have their desires and fears, but they have to provide different de-escalation and different proposals as well, if they want Europe to be able to receive those proposals in a good way," Kushner said at the press conference.

The other side: So far, Russia has been unwilling to allow Europeans to be part of peace talks with Ukraine.

  • "As for the leadership of a number of European countries, they are essentially engaged in a collective deception of the Ukrainian people and contributing to the mass deaths of civilians," Putin adviser Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, said at a press conference after the talks. "Therefore, I don't understand what can be discussed with them."
  • Still, Medinsky said that Russia wants to reach a broader security deal with Europe as part of an agreement to end the war.
  • "In Ukraine, an abscess has simply burst. The entire body needs to be treated — a Band-Aid won't do the trick," he said.

What to watch: The Trump administration wants to negotiate a new Europe-Russia security architecture and a Russia-Ukraine peace deal simultaneously. But the implementation of a security arrangement would only happen after a deal to end the war is reached, according to a source familiar with the White House's thinking.

  • The president of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, said before the talks in Abu Dhabi that Europe will discuss a new security architecture only after the war in Ukraine ends.
  • But two sources with knowledge said European officials who were in Abu Dhabi this week agreed to engage on both tracks simultaneously, while stressing that final decisions on European security architecture would be made only after the war in Ukraine ends.
  • The U.S. hopes giving European representatives a seat at the peace talks will make their governments more willing to discuss and agree on a broader security agreement before the war ends.
  • "Zelensky won't agree to a deal until he knows what happens next regarding security guarantees and Putin wants to know this, too. This is why the security issue is so important," the source said.
  • The source added that the U.S. made it clear to European countries that it would not agree to a security deal with Russia unless Europe and Ukraine are on board. The U.S. also wouldn't give Russia a veto over Europe's security considerations, the source said.

The bottom line: Security will be a key issue at a summit of European leaders in Dublin later this week. European diplomats said the idea of a Russia-Europe security arrangement still faces a lot of resistance and unanswered questions.

item.title: Scoop: Inside Bessent's Situation Room confrontation with Lutnick over China chip security
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over a failure to place Nvidia customer Megaspeed on a list of companies that pose national security concerns, sources familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: The Commerce Department oversees the export of sensitive U.S. technologies and Lutnick's actions — or lack thereof — are increasingly under scrutiny following revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.

Driving the news: At a White House Situation Room meeting on Thursday after the midterm elections, Bessent pressed Lutnick on why Megaspeed had not been added to the Commerce Department's entity list, to which Lutnick responded he would "look into it."

  • Commerce Undersecretary Jeff Kessler also was repeatedly warned about Megaspeed in deputy meetings.
  • But Kessler deferred to Lutnick, saying "That's a decision for the secretary."
  • Sources told Axios that Lutnick has spent the last year "undoing" efforts by other administration officials to hold Megaspeed — a company accused of illegally diverting U.S. chips to China — accountable because of concerns it would escalate the trade war with China.
  • Spokespeople for Treasury couldn't be immediately reached for comment.

The other side: The Commerce Department denied the Situation Room confrontation occurred.

  • "This is false. Secretary Bessent and Secretary Lutnick had no such conversation," spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said.

Catch up quick: The Commerce Department is increasingly at the center of scrutiny over the broader Trump administration's handling of an intelligence memo overseen by State Department head Marco Rubio.

  • Lutnick was among the officials who received the report in May, ahead of a trip to China, Axios first reported.
  • On Tuesday, the New York Times reported Commerce Undersecretary Kessler abruptly stopped an investigation into Megaspeed after Nvidia intervened.
  • The Financial Times reported the department was delaying efforts to blacklist Megaspeed despite several U.S. government agencies pushing it to do so.

Inside the room: White House and intelligence officials have pressed Lutnick and his top advisers to take action against Megaspeed since the fall of 2025, sources tell Axios. But they refused, so Bessent spoke up Thursday.

  • "How come Megaspeed isn't on the entities list?" Bessent asked Lutnick, according to a source briefed on the meeting.
  • Lutnick initially stammered, sources said, and then replied: ""I don't know. I'll look into it."
  • One source, who has extensive experience concerning the chip controversy, said the reply was "bullshit" because Lutnick had resisted action ever since he was personally handed a memo, drafted by National Security Adviser and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that outlined the problems with Megaspeed.

The big picture: Nvidia's AI chips provide the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge artificial intelligence, including systems that could transform warfare and cyberattacks.

Between the lines: The rivalry between Bessent and Lutnick dates to Trump's transition, when both sought the Treasury secretary job. After Trump chose Bessent, the two clashed over trade policy.

  • Bessent's confrontation comes amid a broader slowdown in Commerce's enforcement of U.S. export restrictions, with national security officials increasingly frustrated by decisions to avoid antagonizing China.
  • Blacklisting a company is an interagency decision, with Commerce leading a committee that includes State, Defense and Energy, and consults Treasury when appropriate.
  • Commerce has not added a single company to its Entity List in more than a year, according to a review of the Federal Register, despite mounting pressure from national security officials.

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Don Leonard isn't a House member yet. He's already rocking Capitol Hill.
item.description:
Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) hasn't been sworn in yet, but he's making a name for himself on Capitol Hill as one of the most outspoken anti-establishment progressives in the incoming freshman class.

Why it matters: That's an unlikely position for a Democrat who represents a rural Ohio district that President Trump carried by 10 percentage points in 2024.

  • Leonard is archetypal of a burgeoning breed of swing-district House Democrats — populist in style, receptive to left-wing policies and unbound by traditional political norms — that will be well-represented in the 120th Congress.
  • "I'm really vibing with my class," he told Axios in a Tuesday interview on Capitol Hill. "These are everyday citizens who heard the same call I heard and stood up."

State of play: Leonard, a professor of city planning who defeated Republican Rep. Mike Carey in last Tuesday's midterm elections, was turning heads on Capitol Hill before he even arrived for freshman orientation on Sunday.

  • He told his local CBS affiliate the day after the election he will "be shopping for a new leader" unless House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) changes his pro-Israel positions.
  • He made an even bigger splash on Tuesday with a video he posted to social media saying he met with "senior members" who warned him his life would be a "living hell" and that he would lose reelection if he opposes Jeffries for speaker of the House.

The other side: House Democratic Caucus Chair Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.), asked about Leonard's video at a press conference Tuesday afternoon, told reporters, "I don't know what senior Democrats he's talking about."

  • "I think all of us here can attest to the work, the time, the energy that Hakeem Jeffries put into helping us build this majority," Aguilar said.
  • Aguilar predicted Jeffries will be "overwhelmingly selected" as speaker and that he doesn't "lose any sleep over that."
  • "Members could have ideas and interests and they could have asks along the way, but the outcome is not in question," he added.

What they're saying: Leonard, in his interview with Axios later on Tuesday afternoon, characterized the conversation described in his video as a "friendly" and "well-intentioned" talk with "folks who have been on the Hill for a really long time."

  • "They let me know that while we all agree on a lot of this stuff ... the leader is going to pursue his message and agenda as he sees fit, and [said], 'Don't be insane. How could you possibly stand in the way?'"
  • In addition to cutting U.S. aid for Israel, Leonard said he wants Jeffries to commit to supporting a Constitutional amendment to ban super PACs.
  • "The time for half-measures is over," he told Axios. "I hear people, even members of the Progressive Caucus, talking about, 'Maybe we just tax super PACs.' Y'all, we need a 28th Amendment."

Between the lines: Leonard said he has also found himself irked by House Democrats' seniority system, which makes it difficult for freshman members to get onto some of the most coveted committees.

  • "I'm just a little confused and frustrated right now by why the Democratic caucus is so hierarchical when it comes to these committees," he told Axios.
  • Leonard added: "When we're less democratic than the Republican Party ... that raises questions for me."

What's next: The Ohio Democrat said he got a chance to meet Jeffries for the first time on Tuesday and arrange for their staffers to work out a time to sit down and talk.

  • "I shook his hand and I asked him for six minutes," he said, telling Axios he wants to "look him in the eye, let him know that [I] respect his capacity as a leader ... but I need something to take back to my district that shows that my party understands the magnitude of the crisis we face."
  • "I'm going to hope that I can persuade him in the six minutes that we don't have to cross that bridge, but my constituents aren't bluffing and neither am I."

item.title: Dems put Noem on notice
item.description:
President Trump fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March, but Democrats aren't finished with her.

Why it matters: Armed with commanding House and Senate majorities, they're preparing to haul the architects of Trump's mass deportation agenda before Congress to answer for their actions.

  • "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what's up? Clear your schedule," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, warned on X.
  • She was referencing current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who replaced Noem), White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Border Czar Tom Homan and former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino.
  • Dems on the House Oversight Committee included former DHS Special Government Employee Corey Lewandowski in a list of people who should "lawyer up."

Zoom in: Rep. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, said in a letter to colleagues he'd prioritize investigating every death in DHS custody and during arrests.

  • Thompson, who is running for committee chair and the subpoena power that comes with it, also plans to investigate alleged financial corruption at the agency and oversight of spending, particularly the gargantuan budget supplied by the One Big Beautiful Bill.
  • "I called for Kristi Noem's impeachment in January, and she was gone by March. But the questions she refused to answer are still open," Thompson wrote.
  • "Tom Homan and Stephen Miller would not appear [for a hearing] when we invited them this spring. In the majority, they will not have that choice," he wrote.

Zoom out: Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate have a lengthy list of areas for oversight, according to sources familiar with their plans.

That includes:

  • The billions spent to expand ICE detention, including Alligator Alcatraz and a warehouse buying spree. Oversight agencies have been reviewing these purchases.
  • Noem's purchase of luxury private jets that she claimed could be used for deportation flights. A senior administration official called these purchases "abuse" at the time.
  • Alleged conflicts of interest involving Lewandowski, Noem's top advisor, who was accused of seeking payments from DHS contractors. Lewandowski has long denied wrongdoing. Dems have welcomed reports that the Justice Department was investigating Lewandowski.
  • Use of force incidents involving ICE agents, including fatal shootings. They also want to investigate a whistleblower complaint about how ICE's hiring spree reduced the amount of training new agents received before being put on the streets.

Between the lines: Noem was dismissed from her role in part because of a $200 million DHS ad campaign, starring her.

  • Noem claimed in a congressional hearing that President Trump was aware of the cost of the ad campaign, which encouraged self-deportations.
  • Noem also oversaw a policy of personally signing off on all agency spending over $100,000, creating a bottleneck that slowed down everything from border wall construction to FEMA grants. The agency said at the time the policy fought waste, fraud and abuse.

The other side: DHS declined to share comment from Mullin, who formerly served in both the House and Senate.

  • DHS general counsel James Percival said in response to Ramirez on X, "It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing. Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland."
  • DHS declined to say which oversight priorities Percival considers nonsense.

The White House referred comment on Noem and Lewandowski to DHS, but spokesperson Lauren Bis said of Homan or Miller's potentially being called to testify: "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." DHS did not respond to a follow-up request on Noem or Lewandowski.

  • Bovino, who is now retired, replied to Ramirez on X, "Honey, slow your totalitarian roll. Citizens don't answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that."
  • Lewandowski did not respond to an Axios request for comment.
item.content:encoded:
President Trump fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem in March, but Democrats aren't finished with her.

Why it matters: Armed with commanding House and Senate majorities, they're preparing to haul the architects of Trump's mass deportation agenda before Congress to answer for their actions.

  • "Noem, Markwayne, Miller, Homan, Bovino, what's up? Clear your schedule," Rep. Delia Ramirez (D-Ill.), a member of the House Homeland Security Committee, warned on X.
  • She was referencing current DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin (who replaced Noem), White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, Border Czar Tom Homan and former Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino.
  • Dems on the House Oversight Committee included former DHS Special Government Employee Corey Lewandowski in a list of people who should "lawyer up."

Zoom in: Rep. Bennie Thompson, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee, said in a letter to colleagues he'd prioritize investigating every death in DHS custody and during arrests.

  • Thompson, who is running for committee chair and the subpoena power that comes with it, also plans to investigate alleged financial corruption at the agency and oversight of spending, particularly the gargantuan budget supplied by the One Big Beautiful Bill.
  • "I called for Kristi Noem's impeachment in January, and she was gone by March. But the questions she refused to answer are still open," Thompson wrote.
  • "Tom Homan and Stephen Miller would not appear [for a hearing] when we invited them this spring. In the majority, they will not have that choice," he wrote.

Zoom out: Democratic leaders in both the House and Senate have a lengthy list of areas for oversight, according to sources familiar with their plans.

That includes:

  • The billions spent to expand ICE detention, including Alligator Alcatraz and a warehouse buying spree. Oversight agencies have been reviewing these purchases.
  • Noem's purchase of luxury private jets that she claimed could be used for deportation flights. A senior administration official called these purchases "abuse" at the time.
  • Alleged conflicts of interest involving Lewandowski, Noem's top advisor, who was accused of seeking payments from DHS contractors. Lewandowski has long denied wrongdoing. Dems have welcomed reports that the Justice Department was investigating Lewandowski.
  • Use of force incidents involving ICE agents, including fatal shootings. They also want to investigate a whistleblower complaint about how ICE's hiring spree reduced the amount of training new agents received before being put on the streets.

Between the lines: Noem was dismissed from her role in part because of a $200 million DHS ad campaign, starring her.

  • Noem claimed in a congressional hearing that President Trump was aware of the cost of the ad campaign, which encouraged self-deportations.
  • Noem also oversaw a policy of personally signing off on all agency spending over $100,000, creating a bottleneck that slowed down everything from border wall construction to FEMA grants. The agency said at the time the policy fought waste, fraud and abuse.

The other side: DHS declined to share comment from Mullin, who formerly served in both the House and Senate.

  • DHS general counsel James Percival said in response to Ramirez on X, "It is unfortunate that Democrats are more interested in political shenanigans than in governing. Rest assured, however, that we are well prepared to deal with this nonsense so Secretary Mullin can continue focusing on protecting the homeland."
  • DHS declined to say which oversight priorities Percival considers nonsense.

The White House referred comment on Noem and Lewandowski to DHS, but spokesperson Lauren Bis said of Homan or Miller's potentially being called to testify: "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people." DHS did not respond to a follow-up request on Noem or Lewandowski.

  • Bovino, who is now retired, replied to Ramirez on X, "Honey, slow your totalitarian roll. Citizens don't answer to communists in this country as much as you seem to believe that."
  • Lewandowski did not respond to an Axios request for comment.

item.title: The AI industry's week from hell
item.description:
A week of political upheaval, financial turmoil and salacious scandal delivered one final indignity to the AI industry Tuesday, as Anthropic's staggering IPO target fell short of expectations.

Why it matters: The bubble is wobbling. Investors, businesses and governments need a spectacular success from Anthropic to stave off a crisis of confidence that could tear through the broader economy.

  • Facing new political headwinds, the industry can scarcely afford another setback — much less the spectacle of AI's crown jewel losing its luster on Wall Street.

Zoom in: Anthropic announced plans Tuesday to raise as much as $64.4 billion in one of the largest IPOs in history, targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

  • That's roughly $600 billion below what investors envisioned just months ago, as slowing revenue growth, soaring infrastructure costs and a punishing market selloff tempered expectations.
  • Anthropic's annualized revenue reached $81 billion in October, but its long-term commitments to chips, data centers and computing infrastructure have also climbed to nearly $901 billion.

Zoom out: Anthropic's valuation reset caps a punishing stretch of new challenges that began with last week's stunning midterm results:

🌊 A blue wave of AI-skeptical Democrats will arrive in Congress armed with subpoena power and an appetite for investigating the industry's safety failures and vast political influence.

  • Voters delivered another blow at the local level, favoring restrictions on data-center development in 40 of 41 ballot measures nationwide.

🤖 Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the central cog in AI's global gears, was swept up in an espionage scandal after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. His board, the FBI and Congress are investigating.

  • Nvidia has shed more than $1 trillion in market value since the first New York Times revelations on Oct. 29, with shares plunging further Tuesday as the company faces a new shareholder lawsuit.

📉 Wall Street went into a tailspin as investors reckoned with the implications of the Democratic sweep — including in data-center havens like Texas — for AI's sprawling infrastructure ambitions.

  • The Nasdaq lost $2.5 trillion in market value Thursday, its worst session since April 2025, before staging a sharp rebound.

⚠️ Financial warning signs are mounting: OpenAI scaled back its fundraising ambitions, while SoftBank reported a $3.7 billion write-down on U.S. data-center equipment, contributing to a $7 billion quarterly loss.

  • Amid renewed fears of rate hikes, anxiety is also spreading to credit markets, where lenders have grown wary of financing the industry's astronomical infrastructure spending.

Reality check: Anthropic is still poised for one of the largest IPOs ever, with Google, Nvidia and other technology giants committing another $26 billion in private investment alongside the public offering.

  • The company could emerge with roughly $85 billion in net new capital — a historic financial windfall for a company founded less than six years ago.

Yes, but: Bubbles don't run on "good enough." They demand more, better and faster — indefinitely.

  • Even a $1 trillion or $1.5 trillion valuation of Anthropic may not be enough to reassure investors, who thought just a few weeks ago it'd be worth as much as $2 trillion.

What to watch: Whether Anthropic can deliver a spectacular debut and sustain it after trading begins. SpaceX's stock surged after its record June IPO, only to surrender those gains and fall below its offering price within weeks.

item.title: House GOP bets on MAGA "fighter" Jim Jordan
item.description:
House Republicans are turning to one of their fiercest fighters to lead their diminished conference after one of their biggest drubbings in decades.

Why it matters: Jim Jordan, 62, a founding member of the hardline House Freedom Caucus, has completed a stunning insurgent-to-establishment turn after spending much of his nearly 20 years in Congress battling Republican leaders from the right.

  • The Ohio Republican's victory over House Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) represents a bet by Republicans that they shouldn't move away from President Trump to claw their way back to power.
  • But Republicans are divided over what went wrong in the midterms, and whether a more confrontational approach is the right answer.

Driving the news: Republicans emerged from last week's defeat hungry for change, handing Jordan a 106–73 victory over long-time GOP leader Scalise.

  • GOP Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.) survived their elections.
  • Jordan pitched himself as a battle-tested fighter capable of defending Trump against Democratic investigations and winning back the majority.

What they're saying: "I think when you take a beating like we took, you need to make some changes, and I also think we're gearing up for war," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.), who backed Jordan, told Axios.

  • "We need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Fine said.
  • "We just got beat bad. We can't just go in with the same step forward," Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios.
  • McClain told Axios: "Don't count Jim Jordan out. He's a fighter. He's been able to get stuff done."

Yes, but: Not all Republicans are convinced they have the right response to their losses.

  • Rep. Carlos Gimenez (R-Fla.), who backed Scalise, argued that Republicans lost too many independent and Hispanic voters, pointing specifically to the Trump administration's immigration enforcement policies.
  • Asked whether Republicans should have examined their losses before electing new leaders, Gimenez said: "Yeah, we probably should have," adding he was "not sure" whether Jordan is the right person to lead Republicans back to the majority, though he pledged to support him.
  • "We've got to do a lot of introspection," Rep. Mark Alford (R-Mo.) told Axios. "It's going to take some really deep thought and really looking at what we did wrong and what we can do to gain back the trust of the American people."

Zoom in: Jordan's victory marks a major shift in the relationship between GOP leadership and the hardline House Freedom Caucus, whose members have spent years clashing with party leaders.

  • Rep. Eric Burlison (R-Mo.), who is running to chair the Freedom Caucus, told Axios he hopes the group won't have to push leadership as hard under Jordan, though it will still try to serve as the party's "moral compass."
  • But Rep. Eli Crane (R-Ariz.), a Freedom Caucus member who voted for Jordan, warned that changing the man at the top won't change the conference's ideological divisions.
  • "I still don't expect a ton to change," Crane told Axios.

The intrigue: Jordan's elevation could also sharpen tensions with Senate Republicans, whose leader, John Thune (R-S.D.), has frustrated House Republicans over his handling of Trump's legislative priorities.

  • Asked whether Jordan would push back harder on the Senate than Scalise, Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.) told Axios: "That's to be seen, but I think he was voted in with that in mind."

The bottom line: Jordan inherits a conference eager for a new direction but still deeply divided over what that should look like.

item.title: Scoop — Stephen Miller's post-midterm focus: MAGA and men
item.description:
Stephen Miller wants to use his new role as White House chief of staff to win back young and minority men who helped elect President Trump in 2024 but swung toward Democrats in the midterms, two people familiar with the administration's plans tell Axios.

Why it matters: Miller, named last week to replace Susie Wiles, plans to focus on reviving the populist agenda that helped the president build his 2024 coalition, with an emphasis on working-class voters.

Young, working-class and minority men fled the GOP in droves in last week's elections, amid high prices fueled by Trump's tariffs, the war in Iran, and concerns about AI's impact on the job market.

  • Another key factor in last week's voting: Latino men also swung sharply toward Democrats, as the administration's hard-line immigration crackdown became an increasingly contentious political issue.

Driving the news: Miller wants to spend more time highlighting administration policies he believes haven't gotten enough attention, and that will appeal to working-class voters concerned about the economy, insiders tell Axios.

  • His priorities will sound familiar to Trump watchers: eliminating what the administration considers "woke" policies from colleges and workplaces, lowering prescription drug prices, and rooting out government and health-care fraud.
  • He also wants to emphasize reducing the federal bureaucracy and push for permitting reform, while highlighting how those efforts could help address affordability.
  • Sources in the business community say Miller's ideological drive makes him mostly impervious to typical Washington lobbying.

Yes, but: With Democrats taking control of Congress in January, Miller will have to advance that agenda without the help of Republican majorities in either the House or Senate.

  • Some of his plans could be pursued through executive orders by Trump. Others, including permitting reform, would require bipartisan cooperation.
  • That could be a challenge: Miller, a political fighter who's been called Trump's "wartime consigliere," isn't popular among Democrats.
  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who's in line to become House speaker in January, has said he has "zero interest" in working with Miller, whose immigration policies have made him a frequent target of Democratic attacks.

Flashback: Trump won men under 30 by 14 points in the 2024 election, according to a Tufts University study of election data.

  • Last week, Democrats won that demographic by 22 points in House races — a 36-point shift.
  • The shift was even more pronounced among young Latino men, who went from backing Trump by 2 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 37 points in 2026.
  • Young voters with a high school education or less swung 37 points toward Democrats — from backing Trump by 12 points in 2024 to favoring Democrats by 25 points in the midterms.

More than half of voters under 30 cited the economy and jobs as one of the country's three biggest issues, according to the Tufts study.

  • Among young voters who said they were falling behind financially, 73% backed Democratic House candidates.

Miller's focus on young men isn't new. He made direct appeals to them during Trump's 2024 campaign.

  • During a Fox News appearance just before the 2024 election, he urged young men to embrace their support for Trump, telling them to "show that you are a real man" and "not a beta."
  • On Election Day 2024, Miller posted on X: "Get every man you know to the polls."

item.title: The Democratic leadership revolt has a glaring problem
item.description:
The Republican leadership fights are over. For Democrats, the pain has only just begun.

Why it matters: All the talk about changing party leadership is empty if no one steps up to run.

  • Senate Republicans demanded more time and deeper conversations about their leadership, but no one stepped forward to challenge John Thune, who won by acclamation.
  • Democrats are demanding their own conversations about the party's future and the leadership of Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries. Neither has a challenger.

‼️ The intrigue: Where there was a contested leadership fight, the challenger won.

  • Rep. Jim Jordan, the Freedom Caucus founding member who spent years tormenting Republican leaders, will now lead the battered House GOP after defeating 12-year leadership veteran Rep. Steve Scalise by 33 votes.
  • Jordan is the kind of fighter House Republicans want to take on Democrats as they enter the minority, lawmakers told Axios.
  • "We're gearing up for war. And you're talking to a guy who's known as a hammer. You know we need someone who can punch hard, and I think that he'll do that," Rep. Randy Fine (R-Fla.) told Axios.

🤺 Zoom in: No such fighter has emerged to challenge Democratic leaders from within their ranks, and Schumer said he is "confident I will be elected majority leader."

  • The closest thing to a challenge is Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.), who's listening to calls to run for Democratic leader while also considering a presidential campaign. It's hard to do both.
  • Meanwhile, opposition to Schumer is building: "[T]he time is now for change," Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) said Tuesday. He appeared with Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), who said she's not "actively seeking the job" but demanded a plan for change.

🏛️ Over in the House, Jeffries is dismissive of the idea that anyone would challenge him after the midterms gave him a massive majority.

  • "You think I don't have the vote nailed down? I guess we'll find out next Wednesday," he told reporters on Monday.
  • Some of his new members are signaling that they're not afraid to defy their new leaders. Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio) said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker, "but Rome is burning."
  • But other new members are on Jeffries' side, like Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.) and Cait Conley (D-N.Y.).

🤝 Jeffries also has high-profile progressive incumbents on board, such as Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).

  • "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising?" Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday.

Between the lines: Thune and Jordan don't have much of a relationship; Thune had left the House for the Senate two years before Jordan arrived.

What's next: Senators say they plan to be in the Capitol working on Veterans Day.

  • Thune committed to working more days during the lame-duck session to ensure they leave no judge appointments behind, senators said.

item.title: "Rome is burning": Incoming House Democrats prove unusually willing to defy leaders
item.description:
House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare.

Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger.

  • "My class is huge not because of ... the Democratic Party and its brand but despite it," said Rep.-elect Don Leonard (D-Ohio). "Many of us are outsiders who didn't come up through the machine, don't buy into the conventions."
  • Congressional Progressive Caucus chair Greg Casar (D-Texas) told Axios: "Any members that are new and have just run their elections are going to be very close to where the voters are, and we know the voters are very upset."

State of play: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is on track to become speaker, in part thanks to his rock-solid support among sitting House Democrats.

  • His supporters include high-profile progressives such as Casar and Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Pramila Jayapal (D-Wash.) and Ro Khanna (D-Calif.).
  • "There is one candidate in this race, Hakeem Jeffries, and I think that everyone is far more concerned about what that leadership means, what is it promising," Ocasio-Cortez told reporters on Tuesday.

Things get more spotty when gauging Jeffries' support among incoming freshmen, some of whom have openly declined to commit to supporting his leadership.

  • That includes members of the informal progressive "Bloc," including Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier (D-N.Y.), Melat Kiros (D-Colo.), Claire Valdez (D-N.Y.), Adam Hamawy (D-N.J.) and Chris Rabb (D-Pa.).
  • "As far as I've heard, Jeffries is the only one running," said progressive Rep.-elect Randy Villegas (D-Calif.). "But ... I think we need to see some prioritization of some legislation, particularly around health care, foreign policy and immigration."
  • Some incoming and sitting House Democrats have been flooded with calls and emails urging them not to elect Jeffries speaker, Axios previously reported.

The intrigue: It's not just progressives hesitating to throw their full-throated support behind Jeffries. The list also includes some moderates in districts President Trump carried by double digits in 2024.

  • Said Rep.-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson (D-Nev.), a member of the center-left New Democrat Coalition: "I just won a district that went for Trump two years ago by 14%. … I've got to turn around and show that we're making change."
  • "For anyone running for speaker, that's my message back to them," she added. "It's much more about, like, what can you do for Nevada?"
  • "I'd like to see who's on the ballot," said Rep.-elect Jake Johnson (D-Minn.), a member of both the New Dems and the centrist Blue Dogs. "Until I've had an opportunity to chat, until I've had an opportunity to see who's out there, I'm not making any decisions."

Yes, but: Plenty of freshmen are supporting Jeffries as well.

  • Well-represented in that contingent are incoming members who ran in marquee races with substantial backing from House Democrats' campaign apparatus, including Reps.-elect Marni von Wilpert (D-Calif.), Manny Rutinel (D-Colo.), Denise Powell (D-Neb.), Cait Conley (D-N.Y.) and Rebecca Bennett (D-N.J.).
  • Rep.-elect Zack Mullock (D-N.J.), who didn't have support from the national party, told Axios he is "not making many big splashes" as a new member: "You're going to have pretty strong support for Hakeem, and I'll be part of that support."

Zoom in: Several members, such as Leonard and Rep.-elect Richard Ojeda (D-N.C.), have said they want to see Jeffries commit to a ban on corporate PACs as a prerequisite for voting for him.

  • "We need a 28th Amendment in the year 2028 or before to shut down Elon Musk and corporate money and Israeli lobby money, for that matter," Leonard said.
  • Said Ojeda: "I have hard lines: I want to make sure that we are making sure we are getting big money out of politics. It's time for us to stop allowing the billionaire class to buy our elections."

The bottom line: Leonard said it "aches" his heart to potentially oppose the first Black speaker of the House, but that "Rome is burning."

  • The Ohio Democrat said he needs to be able to tell his districts "the leader shares our sense of urgency for transformational change and is willing to take the size of his caucus and take it for a spin."

House Democrats' incoming freshman class is barely a week old and already threatening to defy party leaders in ways most of their incumbent colleagues wouldn't dare.

Why it matters: It's a dynamic House leaders may have to learn to live with as they integrate a massive group of new members who were swept into office on a wave of populist, anti-establishment anger.

item.title: Scoop: Commerce Department received national security warning on Nvidia CEO affair
item.description:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was sent a highly classified memo warning about Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, multiple sources familiar told Axios.

Why it matters: Lutnick oversees the agency charged with keeping sensitive U.S. technology out of the hands of American adversaries. The warning raises questions about how the department weighed potential security risks as it cleared advanced Nvidia chip sales to China-affiliated entities.

Driving the news: Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo detailing Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence officials believe is a Chinese intelligence agent, according to The New York Times.

  • The memo, which drew on surveillance of Alice Huang and a chip-smuggling investigation into her company, Megaspeed, circulated before President Trump's May 13–15 trip to China.
  • Rubio also warned Trump directly aboard Air Force One before a refueling stop in Anchorage where Jensen Huang joined the delegation. He hadn't initially been invited to participate, the Times reported Tuesday.
  • On May 14, Reuters reported that the Commerce Department had cleared around 10 Chinese companies to purchase Nvidia's H200 chips.
  • Some export approvals predated the warning. Nvidia disclosed in February it had received an H200 export license, and Huang told Axios' Ina Fried in March the company had licenses covering Chinese customers.

Yes, but: It's unclear how those approvals ultimately translated into sales, as China's government has halted some chip-buying activity in spite of U.S. approvals.

  • Megaspeed purchased billions of dollars' worth of Nvidia chips, according to multiple media outlets.

What they're saying: Trump said on Monday that it was possible intelligence officials had shown it to him, but he didn't recall: "Certainly, it didn't make much of an impact on me."

  • The Commerce Department did not comment.

Catch up quick: Nvidia has been rocked by the scandal, losing about $1 trillion in market value since the Times' first reported the relationship, although some of that decline also came after an overwhelming number of Democrats promising to slow an AI data-center buildout were elected in the midterms.

  • Huang acknowledged an affair Sunday, and Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation. The board expressed confidence in his leadership and said it had no reason to believe national security secrets were compromised.

What to watch: New revelations continue to drop almost daily about the administration's handling of the Nvidia CEO's relationship. Lawmakers in both parties have promised investigations and demanded more information, including closed-door testimony from Jensen Huang next week.

  • Top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs committee have also demanded answers from Lutnick about the administration's chip approvals, "including to companies with concerning links to China and amid alarming reports of potential Chinese intelligence ties to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang."

item.title: Trump swung between war and diplomacy — then chose a third way
item.description:
When Secretary of State Marco Rubio met with his G7 counterparts in Paris on Tuesday, he told them that President Trump had considered resuming the war with Iran or cutting a deal — but chose a third option: strangling the Iranian regime, three people who attended the meeting told Axios.

Why it matters: The Iran war has become a political albatross in Trump's second term, costing Republicans dearly in the midterms. For months, the president has alternated between threatening to obliterate Iran and predicting it will capitulate and give him the deal he wants.

  • "He's been searching for the solution, but he wasn't sure what's the best way to go," a U.S. official close to Trump said.
  • This debate over which course to follow has led to strife between several factions within the top echelon of the administration. Each faction had the support of U.S. allies in the Middle East — namely Israel favoring renewed strikes and most Gulf countries opposing them.

Driving the news: After meeting with the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani on Monday, Trump said that a new round of strikes against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary."

  • Trump said he instead favors continuing the economic crackdown and naval blockade against Iran, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology.

Behind the scenes: Rubio explained the U.S. Iran policy in a closed meeting on Tuesday with the foreign ministers of the G7 countries in Paris.

  • "The President doesn't just have two options. It's not just return to war or sign a ridiculous peace deal.  We won't do a stupid deal. The third option we have is to continue to do what we do now," Rubio said, according to three people in the room.
  • Rubio went on to say that the U.S. is imposing devastating costs on Iran's economy, making it harder for it to fund terrorist organizations or rebuild its military. And there's no end date.
  • "The President is not under false time pressure, the Iranians are inflicting major damage on their own economy," Rubio said.

The intrigue: U.S. officials say that Rubio was among the members of Trump's national security team who pushed for the strangulation strategy, along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Jared Kushner, Trump's adviser and son-in-law.

  • That group opposed the resumption of war, didn't believe Iran's current positions could lead to a deal that serves U.S. interests and lobbied for the third option.

State of play: Rubio is deeply skeptical of a diplomatic breakthrough.

  • "Iran would love a deal.  The problem is the conditions they continue to place are absurd.  Like, they're not even serious right now," he told reporters after the G7 meeting. 
  • That could change if the Iranians feel more economic pain, he said. "Eventually you have to eat," he said. "Eventually the economic realities penetrate the skull of even the most radical lunatic. So I think as time goes on that will have an impact."

Yes, but: Several U.S. allies — such as Turkey, Iraq and Pakistan — are concerned about Trump's intention to prolong the economic squeeze, a U.S. official said.

  • The person said those allies worry that U.S. pressure on them to stop doing business with Iran — including by stopping flights and closing their borders — will create instability in their own countries.

The other side: The course Trump has chosen is completely at odds with the directive Iran's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei gave his government and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

  • Khamenei ordered an end to the "no war, no deal" status quo, demanding a clear conclusion to the war. Iran's civilian leadership interpreted this as a green light to negotiate a deal.
  • But if the current stalemate continues and pressure on Iran intensifies, the IRGC could see it as a green light for more aggressive attacks in the region in an attempt to break the status quo.
  • "Iran has no intention of simply accepting this situation indefinitely," said Danny Citrinowicz, an expert on Iran at the Atlantic Council. "Tehran may conclude that increasing the economic and security costs for Washington and its regional partners is the only way to force a change in American policy."
  • He added: "The danger is obvious: Iran escalates, Washington responds, and both sides find themselves in another military confrontation that neither necessarily wanted."

What to watch: Qatar's prime minister briefed the G7 meeting on mediation efforts and his conversation with Trump the previous day.

  • Al Thani said he came away from his meeting with Trump believing there's more breathing room for diplomatic efforts.
  • The sticking points remain which side will take the first step toward de-escalating and which confidence-building measures the parties will agree to take.
  • The Qatari prime minister said he wants to bring in China and European countries as guarantors, to help ease deep Iranian suspicions that Trump will break the agreement and resume the war in a few months.

item.title: GOP House rejects Hegseth impeachment effort
item.description:
House Republicans voted Tuesday evening to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, shielding a top Trump administration official from a politically embarrassing rebuke.

Why it matters: The vote marks a victory for Hegseth, the Trump administration and Republican leaders, who were bracing for the prospect of a rebellion within their own ranks.

  • But the reprieve is probably short-lived: Democrats are all but guaranteed to force the issue again when they retake majorities in the House and Senate in January.
  • The vote to refer the impeachment measure back to committee passed 211-204, with Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.), the measure's sponsor, the lone GOP "no" vote.

Driving the news: Massie forced a procedural vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth, alleging he has defied Congress and illegally continued the U.S. war in Iran.

  • The Trump administration has been vehemently defending Hegseth, including through a statement opposing the impeachment effort issued shortly before the vote.
  • "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X.

"Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements," Vance added.

  • Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt previously reported that Hegseth is on "thin ice" with Trump officials.

Between the lines: Republican leaders protected their members from having to go on record on the politically difficult issue before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) sent lawmakers home early to campaign.

What's next: Tuesday's vote effectively kills any effort to impeach Hegseth this Congress.

item.title: Credit card debt hits record high as Americans struggle with cost-of-living
item.description:
Federal Reserve Bank of New York; Note: Not adjusted for inflation; Chart: Axios Visuals

Americans' credit card balances hit a record $1.29 trillion in the third quarter, according to a new report released by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Why it matters: Falling behind on credit card payments can trap struggling households in a cycle of fees, damaged credit and increasingly expensive borrowing. The latest figures show that financial pain is concentrated in lower-income communities, even as delinquency rates improve nationally.

By the numbers: Consumer credit card balances rose by $22 billion in the third quarter, an increase of 1.7%. That's $52 billion higher than a year earlier.

  • The figures aren't adjusted for inflation, meaning some of the increase reflects higher prices rather than greater borrowing in real terms.
  • Total household debt, including mortgages and student and auto loans, rose $334 billion, reaching a record $19.1 trillion in the third quarter. The total is up $5 trillion since 2019, just before the pandemic.

Yes, but: Fewer credit card balances are becoming seriously delinquent, a sign of some improvement in Americans' ability to keep up with payments.

  • The rate at which credit card debt becomes seriously overdue edged down to 6.9% in the third quarter, though it remains notably above the 5.2% recorded before the pandemic.

Between the lines: A separate report from the New York Fed on Tuesday showed Americans in lower-income neighborhoods are having a harder time keeping up with credit card payments relative to their wealthier counterparts.

  • Delinquency rates remain above pre-pandemic levels across all neighborhood-income groups, with the gap between the richest and poorest areas increasing since 2022.
  • In the lowest-income neighborhoods, 10.3% of credit card balances became seriously delinquent over the past year — more than double the 4.4% rate in the wealthiest neighborhoods.

The big picture: Average credit card balance per borrower is now $6,678, according to TransUnion's Q3 insights report.

  • Borrowers under 30 had the highest rate of credit card debt newly becoming at least 90 days overdue, the Fed's report found.

What we're watching: Democrats won the midterms promising to lower prices — but delivering relief that voters can actually feel in their household budgets will be difficult to fulfill.

item.title: Jim Jordan wins House GOP minority leader race
item.description:
House Republicans elected Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) as their new leader Tuesday, handing the reins of the battered GOP conference to one of its most prominent conservative firebrands.

Why it matters: Jordan's victory marks a major shake-up in House Republican leadership, elevating a founding member of the hardline Freedom Caucus who campaigned as an alternative to the leaders who presided over the GOP's crushing midterm defeat.

  • Jordan bested Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.), who had served as the No. 2 House Republican since 2014, in the conference-wide secret ballot for minority leader.
  • Scalise trailed Jordan by 33 votes.
  • Jordan's victory signals an appetite among House Republicans for a more confrontational approach as they prepare to enter the minority.

State of play: Jordan and Scalise entered Tuesday's election locked in a tight race, with both camps expressing confidence in their chances of winning.

  • Jordan drew public support from some of the conference's most conservative members, who argued Republicans needed a change in direction after their devastating midterm losses.
  • Scalise leaned on his longstanding relationships across the conference and his decade-plus of experience in leadership.

The big picture: Jordan's ascent represents a remarkable turnaround for a conservative agitator who spent much of his career challenging the Republican establishment before becoming one of President Trump's most vocal allies.
