item.title: 3 charged with plotting terror attacks in U.S., Europe
item.description:
Three individuals were charged in connection with alleged Iranian-linked terror plots, including a September scheme against a British Royal Air Force Base that housed U.S. military personnel and aircraft, per an indictment unsealed Tuesday.

The big picture: The indictment alleges that a leader of an Islamic terrorist group attempted to coordinate with his fellow defendants from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

  • The charges include conspiracy to provide material support to a Foreign Terrorist Organization, conspiracy to provide material support for acts of terrorism, attempted acts of terrorism across national boundaries and conspiracy to bomb a place of public use, among others.

Driving the news: Since early in the year, the three men named in the indictment worked to commit terror attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, the indictment alleges.

  • The eight-count superseding indictment names Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national. It highlights nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks, which included plots against Jewish institutions in Europe and the U.S.
  • Al-Saadi was charged in May for working with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah, both of which the U.S. has designated as Foreign Terrorist Organizations.

What's inside: Even after al-Saadi was arrested and transferred to U.S. custody, he allegedly passed coded messages to his fellow defendants in the days leading up to an attempted plot targeting the RAF Fairford base in England.

  • The U.K. earlier this year allowed the U.S. to use RAF Fairford for limited defensive strikes against Iranian missile capabilities, elevating the base's position on the IRGC's radar.
  • Al-Hassani and Mohajeri were in Iran at the time, but relied on a network of contacts in the U.K. whom Al-Hassani allegedly paid to prepare by acquiring vans and barrels of fuel and researching chemical accelerants in preparation for the Fairford attack, the indictment says.

Catch up quick: British police arrested five men on suspicion of terrorism near the base back in September.

  • Iran denied any involvement in the suspected plot at the time, Axios previously reported.

What they're saying: "Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy," Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor said in a statement.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional information.

item.title: The Atlantic can pursue FBI records in fight with Kash Patel
item.description:
A federal judge took sharp aim at FBI Director Kash Patel on Tuesday, ruling in favor of The Atlantic and freezing most discovery in his defamation lawsuit against the publication.

Why it matters: The ruling shields The Atlantic from potentially intrusive demands for its reporting materials and confidential sources while the court weighs dismissing the case entirely.

Driving the news: "Plaintiff misrepresents Defendants' argument, the court's reasoning in Moldea, and the standard applicable in this District," U.S. District Judge Emmet Sullivan wrote in his 16-page ruling.

  • "The Court concludes that discovery should be stayed at this juncture because of Defendants' legitimate First Amendment concerns and because discovery may be unnecessary," Sullivan wrote.

Catch up quick: Patel sued The Atlantic after the magazine reported in April that he allegedly drinks excessively and is sometimes unavailable or difficult for his staff to wake because he was seemingly intoxicated.

  • The story also alleged that Patel had grown increasingly worried about losing his job.
  • Patel denied the reporting and sued the publication shortly after the story aired.

What they're saying: "The judge's ruling in favor of The Atlantic today is a significant procedural victory in our defense against this meritless lawsuit," a spokesperson for the publication told Axios in an emailed statement.

  • "The Atlantic's legal counsel will immediately begin the process of seeking factual discovery from the FBI and the Department of Justice––including documents and depositions of key individuals. As we said this summer: If Director Patel did not want to face this process, he should not have filed this suit."

Zoom in: The judge paused most discovery until he rules on The Atlantic's motion to dismiss the lawsuit, but both sides may request government records.

  • The Atlantic says it needs Justice Department and FBI records to assess the truth of its reporting and Patel's reputation.
  • Patel complained the requests were too broad, seeking everything from his medical and travel records to his calendar and records about personnel decisions.
  • Sullivan rejected Patel's objection that the arrangement was unfair.

The intrigue: The Atlantic warned that discovery could involve "the sitting FBI Director invading Defendants' newsgathering and editorial processes," potentially exposing confidential sources to retaliation.

  • The Atlantic called Patel a "serial defamation plaintiff" and warned that he "may seek to wield governmental power" in connection with the lawsuit and broader criticism of his FBI leadership.
  • Sullivan agreed that the magazine had "legitimate First Amendment concerns" and found it would face "substantial prejudice" if discovery proceeded now.

Worth noting: Sullivan didn't rule on whether the Atlantic's reporting is true or whether Patel was defamed.

  • The FBI didn't immediately respond to Axios' request for comment.

Go deeper: Kash Patel files $250M defamation lawsuit against The Atlantic

Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from The Atlantic.

item.title: Vance says Hegseth impeachment vote "isn't about Iran"
item.description:
Vice President JD Vance on Tuesday said that the vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "isn't about Iran," but rather his willingness to take on challenges at the Pentagon.

Why it matters: It's the latest instance of the Trump administration backing the embattled Cabinet member, who is facing the possibility of enough GOP members defecting for the impeachment effort to succeed.

  • The Iran war is at the center of the allegations against Hegseth, with three of the eight articles of impeachment specifically concerning the conflict.
  • Other allegations include that Hegseth illegally initiated military conflict in Venezuela and Yemen.

What they're saying: "Has Pete Hegseth committed impeachable crimes? The question is absurd and the answer is: obviously not," Vance said Tuesday on X.

  • "Like so much of Congress, impeachment has become a ridiculous show that stands in for actual policymaking. Congress has so many tools for registering its policy disagreements."
  • Vance added that Congress was choosing to impeach Hegseth as they did President Trump. "Legislation is hard. Impeachments are easy (and ultimately, inconsequential)."
  • "The irony is that legislators are most angry at Pete on the issues where he's most correct: repositioning forces away from Europe/Ukraine and reorganizing the general officer corps," he continued. "This isn't about Iran, this is about the fact that Pete took on the bureaucracy at the Pentagon."

Catch up quick: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-KY) introduced articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, potentially setting the stage for the first impeachment of a Cabinet Secretary during Trump's second term and signaling possible future efforts when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

  • Though Republicans previously resisted efforts to constrain the administration's military operations in Iran, some may be more willing to back Hegseth's impeachment after voters signaled strong disapproval of the administration and the Iran war during the midterm elections.
  • Hegseth likened Massie's push to oust him to Democrats' successful impeachments of President Trump, saying the president was impeached over a "perfect phone call."

What we're watching: The U.S. House is scheduled to hold a preliminary impeachment vote Tuesday afternoon, but even if Congress impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Republican-controlled Senate.

Go deeper: Hegseth faces impeachment resolution from GOP member with little to lose

Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

item.title: Harsh new inflation reality
item.description:
America's inflation problem is stubborn, broadening out and showing no sign of letting up.

Why it matters: October marked the third straight month of hotter-than-expected inflation, defying repeated predictions over the last couple of years that price pressures were finally about to ease.

  • In this sixth consecutive year of steep price increases, consumers are finding there is nowhere to hide from inflation.
  • The Iran war has added to the pain, but other factors — tariffs and the AI investment boom — have also put upward pressure on costs, complicating an affordability problem that long predates the conflict.

What they're saying: "Today's inflation report is a warning shot," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, wrote Tuesday morning.

  • "Coming just a week after the midterm elections exposed the depth of voters' concerns about affordability, the message for the Fed is uncomfortable but clear: The inflation fight is not finished," Shah wrote.

Driving the news: The headline Consumer Price Index rose 0.4% in October, down slightly from a 0.6% surge the previous month.

  • Core CPI — which excludes volatile food and energy costs — climbed 0.3% for the third consecutive month, a sign that underlying inflationary pressures remain stubbornly persistent.

The Labor Department did not calculate October's annual inflation rate since last year's government shutdown prevented it from collecting price data for October 2025.

  • But assuming prices that month were halfway between September and November, overall inflation over the last 12 months was 4% — up from 3.7% in September. Core inflation would have risen to 2.8%, up from 2.6%.
  • Another measure similarly paints a picture of hot inflation. Core prices rose at a 3.7% annualized pace over the three months through October, the fastest pace by this gauge all year.
  • It also is a sharp acceleration from the summer, when underlying inflation appeared to be cooling.

Zoom out: Gasoline prices advanced another 1% in October after surging 9.1% in September, adding to the steep increase in fuel costs since the Iran war began.

  • Food prices climbed, raising concerns that higher diesel costs are rippling through to consumer prices. Grocery prices increased 0.4% after declining in September, while restaurant prices gained 0.5%.
  • Shelter costs rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the overall increase in consumer prices last month.

Zoom in: Inflation is persistent in the services sector, which is largely insulated from swings in energy prices.

  • A closely watched inflation measure that excludes housing, energy and food prices surged 0.4% in October — pushed up by higher costs in transportation, medical care and insurance.

What to watch: A strong labor market is not providing much relief from the sharply rising cost of living.

  • Inflation has now outpaced or matched wage growth for three consecutive months, leaving workers with less purchasing power.

item.title: Pressure builds on Thune ahead of GOP leadership elections
item.description:
Eight Republican senators now are calling for their leadership elections to be delayed — with one even promising to walk out rather than vote Tuesday.

Why it matters: Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) is still expected to be reelected to lead the Senate GOP tomorrow. But the growing push to delay is a sign of troubles ahead.

What we're hearing: Senate Republicans spent roughly two hours behind closed doors hashing out their path forward.

  • Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisc.) led much of the conversation, arguing for a delay in the leadership elections and demanding an aggressive lame duck schedule, senators told Axios.
  • Some senators also discussed their election losses, including Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). Both were ousted last week.
  • They will resume the discussion at 2pm ET, where leadership votes — and motions to delay leadership elections — are expected.

Driving the news: Sens. Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) plan to float a delay of the leadership vote by one week during a morning, closed-door GOP meeting, according to a source directly familiar with their plans.

  • Meanwhile Johnson's group of five senators who wrote a letter calling for a delay will bring a motion to delay the vote by a whole month.
  • Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) emerged from Tuesday's closed-door morning meeting telling reporters he planned to vote for a delay.
  • Some senators see Senate GOP Whip John Barrasso (R-Wyo.) as a better option for leader. Barrasso won't raise his hand for the position unless Thune decides not to run.

Catch up quick: Johnson, Rick Scott (R-Fla.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Ted Budd (R-N.C.) and John Kennedy (R-La.) all signed a letter demanding that the leadership elections be delayed to allow for more discussion about what went wrong for the party last week.

  • McCormick and Banks backed them up in statements posted on X.
  • Johnson threatened to skip the vote if the delay doesn't happen.

Between the lines: The decision technically falls to conference chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) — though it's usually made with leadership buy-in.

  • The election is expected to be held as planned Tuesday morning unless a senator motions to delay and it passes with a majority — which seems unlikely given the number of senators who have publicly called for a later vote, according to a source familiar with the planning discussions.

The bottom line: At this point, none of the leadership elections are competitive.

  • No one has thrown their hat in the ring to challenge Thune.
  • And Barrasso, Cotton, Policy Committee Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) and Conference Vice Chair James Lankford (R-Okla.) are expected to keep their spots as Nos. 2, 3, 4 and 5 atop the conference.
  • Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) is the sole candidate for NRSC chair.

Editor's note: This article has been updated with more reporting.

item.title: Price pressures persisted in October
item.description:
Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios

Inflation remained hot in October, according to data from the Labor Department released on Tuesday.

Why it matters: The Consumer Price Index shows that even as gasoline prices steadied, inflation pressures elsewhere remained stubborn.

By the numbers: CPI rose 0.4% last month, slowing from the 0.6% increase in September.

  • Gasoline prices gained 1% in October, a sharp slowdown from the 9.1% surge in September, the Labor Department said.
  • Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, advanced 0.3% for the third straight month, with higher prices for recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares contributing to the increase.

Of note: The Labor Department did not publish year-over-year inflation rates for October. Last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data that prevents direct comparisons with October 2025.

  • But if one assumes the October 2025 readings were halfway between September and November, year-over-year inflation comes to 4% — or 2.8% excluding food and energy.
  • That compares with September's annual inflation rate of 3.7%, or 2.6% excluding food and energy.

The big picture: The inflation report was already shaping up to be a crucial piece of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next month. But the stakes grew just hours before its release when Fed governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual rate hike if inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

  • In a speech, Fed governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate hike should be considered next month if core inflation rose by at least 0.3% in October — exactly what Tuesday's report showed.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rate policy, jumped 0.13% on Tuesday following Waller's comments and the CPI report.

What to watch: The report also offers a fresh measure of the inflation problem that helped shape last week's midterm elections.

  • Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote in last week's midterms, according to national exit polling data.
  • Democrats won on promises to lower prices for groceries and other essentials. Now they face the more difficult task of delivering on their promises, with limited power to reverse years of price increases.

The bottom line: Inflation remains stubbornly hot, strengthening the case for another Fed rate hike and prolonging the cost-of-living pressures that have frustrated American households.

Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details.

  • Core CPI, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, advanced 0.3% for the third straight month, with higher prices for recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares contributing to the increase.

Of note: The Labor Department did not publish year-over-year inflation rates for October. Last year's government shutdown left a gap in the data that prevents direct comparisons with October 2025.

  • But if one assumes the October 2025 readings were halfway between September and November, year-over-year inflation comes to 4% — or 2.8% excluding food and energy.
  • That compares with September's annual inflation rate of 3.7%, or 2.6% excluding food and energy.

The big picture: The inflation report was already shaping up to be a crucial piece of the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision next month. But the stakes grew just hours before its release when Fed governor Christopher Waller raised the prospect of a larger-than-usual rate hike if inflation remains stubbornly elevated.

  • In a speech, Fed governor Christopher Waller said a half-point rate hike should be considered next month if core inflation rose by at least 0.3% in October — exactly what Tuesday's report showed.
  • The yield on the two-year Treasury note, which is particularly sensitive to expectations for Fed interest rate policy, jumped 0.13% on Tuesday following Waller's comments and the CPI report.

What to watch: The report also offers a fresh measure of the inflation problem that helped shape last week's midterm elections.

  • Nearly nine in 10 voters said the cost of living was a "crucial" or "major" factor in their vote in last week's midterms, according to national exit polling data.
  • Democrats won on promises to lower prices for groceries and other essentials. Now they face the more difficult task of delivering on their promises, with limited power to reverse years of price increases.

The bottom line: Inflation remains stubbornly hot, strengthening the case for another Fed rate hike and prolonging the cost-of-living pressures that have frustrated American households.

item.title: Hegseth comes out swinging against Massie impeachment push
item.description:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth lambasted Rep. Thomas Massie's (R-Ky.) push to oust him, likening the impeachment effort to Democrats' successful impeachments of President Trump.

The big picture: As the possible first impeachment of a Cabinet secretary during the second Trump era and a Democratic-led Congress loom, Hegseth isn't going down without a war of words.

  • Hegseth's news conference was less than 30 minutes long, including the questions he fielded from generally friendly outlets.
  • The conference clearly pleased Trump, who gave Hegseth "an 'A' PLUS, PLUS, PLUS" in a Truth Social post.

Driving the news: "They impeached President Trump over a perfect phone call. They impeached him again in his final week in office," Hegseth said, referencing Trump's first impeachment over a phone call where he pressed Ukraine to investigate Joe Biden and his second over the Jan. 6 attack.

  • "Both times he came back stronger, and the American people sent him back to the White House. Now they're trying a third time. This time against a member of his Cabinet," he continued.
  • "They will fail again, and if standing with President Trump puts me in that company, I'll take that company every day of the week."

Catch up quick: Massie, who Hegseth labeled a "disgruntled congressman," introduced his articles of impeachment against the defense secretary Monday over his handling of the war in Iran and other alleged misconduct.

  • Republicans who were defeated in last week's stunning midterm shakeup have little left to lose and could get on board with impeaching Hegseth, Axios previously reported. Post-election attendance could also be an issue.

What he's saying: Hegseth mounted a defense of scrutinized U.S. military operations in Iran, Venezuela and the Caribbean.

  • "We sank the boats carrying poison into our communities. We put a narco dictator in handcuffs. These are not high crimes. This is the job, and it's the job well done," he said.
  • Massie condemned the boat strikes on alleged drug smugglers in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific in his resolution, alleging Hegseth "arrogated to himself and the Executive Branch the roles of judge, jury, and executioner." The operation has killed well over 200 people.
  • Massie's resolution included eight charges, including the accusation that he violated the 1973 War Powers Resolution in connection with the war in Iran and that he retaliated against Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) for his constitutionally protected speech.

What we're watching: Hegseth's impeachment would be monumental. The House has only impeached two Cabinet secretaries in U.S. history.

Go deeper: Why Pete Hegseth could fall through "thin ice"

item.title: The path ahead for the permitting bill
item.description:
The Senate's bipartisan permitting bill advanced in a lopsided vote on Monday, but key hurdles lie ahead.

Why it matters: The legislation could have far-reaching consequences for how energy projects get built across the U.S.

A few takeaways from Monday's vote:

The big margin was politically lopsided. The 73-25 split to advance the bill "was as good or a little bit better" than what co-author Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.) was expecting, she told reporters in the Capitol.

  • The GOP split was 51-1 in favor, with only Sen. Mike Rounds (S.D.) voting no.
  • 21 Democrats and Maine independent Sen. Angus King voted yes, while 23 Dems and independent Sen. Bernie Sanders were against advancing the bill toward full debate.

It was tentative. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) said in a statement afterward that he has "outstanding concerns" with the bill that he'll "fight to address" through amendments.

  • He's not alone in only a tentative yes vote. For instance, Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) is against final passage unless changes to the National Historic Preservation Act are jettisoned, citing tribal concerns.
  • Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) is in a similar place.

Climate hawk vs. climate hawk. The most outspoken Senate Democrats on climate change split on the vote.

  • Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) joined coauthors Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) and Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.) in backing the measure.
  • But Sens. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) and Ed Markey (D-Mass.), along with Sanders, all voted no.

Watch the clock. Whitehouse pledged a "very healthy" amendment process. But the Senate is now up against the lame duck calendar, and the House would still need to act on whatever emerges.

  • Plus, any changes would need to thread a political needle of maintaining Democratic support without losing too many Republicans.

Climate's cachet has fallen. Heinrich and Whitehouse, at a pre-vote press conference, emphasized affordability, data center accountability and jobs before touting power sector emissions curbs from the bill.

  • But Whitehouse also sought to reassure climate and environmental organizations.
  • "This bill is the floor, not the ceiling, of our climate and environmental aspirations, and we look forward to working to accomplish big things with our big Democratic majorities," he said in the Capitol.

President Trump is a wild card. His comments shortly before Monday's vote that he would not approve wind turbines, while reiterating his full support for the bill, rocketed around the Capitol.

  • And the White House reaffirmed that the president "stands 100%" behind the bill.
  • The bill's success depends on Trump officials "getting wind turbines up and spinning to get affordable energy on the grid," and progress is needed before final passage, Whitehouse said in a statement.

What we're watching: Proposed amendments as they roll in, but also the politics in the closely divided House.

  • House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) criticized the bill last week and called for more engagement with his caucus.
  • Asked Monday whether the Senate co-authors' revisions addressed his concerns, Jeffries told reporters that it's still under review.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Trump plans imperial final act to his presidency
item.description:
President Trump, with the clock ticking and congressional investigators closing in, plans to govern even more imperially, hell-bent on stretching executive power, targeting those on his enemies list, pardoning allies, and daring the courts and Congress to slow him down.

Why it matters: Trump and his allies are exploring executive action on new tariffs and immigration restrictions, and asserting greater control over spending. On X over the weekend, Trump discussed targeting and perhaps jailing Democrats who investigate administration officials. He claimed politically motivated harassment.

Trump is retooling his White House by elevating the one official who's synonymous with his all-gas-no-brakes style: Stephen Miller, who took over for Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff on Monday.

  • Watch Miller and Russ Vought, the White House budget director, to understand how this approach will unfold. Both are architects and advocates of vastly expanding presidential power, believing there are virtually no restraints on what Trump can do as president.
  • The Swamp can expect tougher sledding: Miller, unlike most of his predecessors, is driven more by ideology than by meetings with lobbyists or industry groups. "Stephen gives zero f*cks what K Street thinks," a Trump confidant told us.

Between the lines: Midterm losses pushed Presidents Clinton and Obama to the center. Trump's instincts are the opposite: Assert maximal power. The playbook:

  1. Restore MAGA. Two years ago, MAGA — mostly its network of podcasts, YouTubers and online activists — was a powerful, united force in media and politics. Today it's a hot, divided mess. Trump's attention to his base drifted. Now Vice President Vance and Miller desperately want to rebuild and rev up MAGA. That's why ending the Iran war, curtailing aid to Israel and pushing harder on RFK Jr.'s MAHA agenda are suddenly top-tier topics.
  2. Rule by pen. Miller, Vought and White House lawyers have been drafting executive actions to govern without Congress, with Justice Department opinions ready to defend them, Reuters reported just before the election. Remember: Vought was an architect of the Heritage Foundation's Project 2025 blueprint for maximizing executive power in Trump II.
  3. Target enemies. Before, it was pure payback. Now, it's also a preemptive warning that the Trump administration will target anyone, including elected members of Congress who target them. Trump ally Roger Stone told us: "Many Democrat lawmakers are going to find themselves under indictment and fighting conviction. Watch."
  4. Purge the "deep state." The Supreme Court's ruling in a case about independent agencies, Trump v. Slaughter, widened the president's power to remove officials. "The Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers," Trump said in an Election Day phone interview with CBS News' Robert Costa. The June ruling handed Trump the power to fire the heads of the FTC and other independent regulators (like FERC) for any reason or no reason.
  5. More monuments. Trump's pharaonic need to gild the White House, build a ballroom, erect a triumphal arch and slap his name on buildings is also an exercise in raw power. He told New York Magazine's Ben Terris why he's honoring himself: "Nobody will do it once I'm gone. When I leave here, nobody will." No one can stop him.

The Republican resistance: Expect very little inside the new Congress. The reason: Most of Trump's Capitol Hill critics are gone. What's left is a much smaller, but more Trumpian, band of middle-aged and older white Republicans with margins too small to matter much.

  • The Trump bet: Congressional Republicans will quickly feel Democrats are overreaching and unify in solidarity with Trump, even if it's forced or begrudging.

Yes, but: One of Trump's most predictable attributes is his unpredictability. He said on election night that he'll "work together" with Democrats. What that may look like (with a heavy emphasis on "may"), based on reporting by Axios' Marc Caputo:

  1. Soften aspects of immigration enforcement, particularly regarding masked agents harassing U.S. citizens.
  2. Find common ground with MAHA's healthy food agenda, which has become the subject of vicious post-election infighting among Trump insiders.
  3. Sign legislation from the new Congress that would undo massive Medicaid cuts in his "One Big Beautiful Bill."

The bottom line: Trump is still Trump. He's 80 and it shows. But he meets force with force and he'll go down swinging the more Democrats attack him.

  • "Trump and his team are at our best when our backs are against the wall," one adviser told Caputo. "Trump comes out fighting. We're full-throated and full-throttle."

Go deeper: Texas, Texas, Texas.

item.title: How a MAHA leader turned and torched the White House
item.description:
Calley Means quickly rose from wellness entrepreneur to senior Trump health adviser — and now he's attacking the White House and suggesting top aides undermined the president's health agenda.

Why it matters: His scorched-earth campaign — which continued Monday in comments to Axios — marks a stunning turn for a figure who was the administration's most vocal advocate of the "Make America Healthy Again" agenda.

  • It also raises questions about what the escalating fight between Means and former White House officials will accomplish for the movement.

Driving the news: Means told Axios he's going public with his allegations of corruption — especially by former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles — because of the high stakes.

  • "It is existential to the survival [of] America that we rid DC of Susie's brand of politics," Means said in a text exchange.
  • Means' initial comments on Friday's episode of "The Joe Rogan Experience" went viral, and he continued the campaign with an appearance on CBS' "Face the Nation" Sunday.
  • Asked if he's worried about lawsuits after comments from a Wiles spokesperson and former White House deputy chief of staff James Blair — who Means has also accused of wrongdoing — Means pointed to his X post warning them and other parties to "immediately preserve all potentially relevant records and communications."

Means has kept up a steady stream of X posts about his allegations and the way he claims the officials have responded to them.

  • "Susie - I'm not intimidated and you will not scare me. Again, please stop sending me emotional texts. This is not personal - this is civilizational," Means posted Monday.
  • White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said in a statement the Trump administration has won "extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda." The Department of Health and Human Services and a Wiles spokesperson didn't respond to requests for comment.

The big picture: After hitching their wagon to President Trump ahead of the 2024 election, MAHA leaders have been complaining for months of a lack of progress on issues around healthy foods and pesticide use.

  • But whether the public feud Means has initiated will have any impact on the policy agenda he's championed — or whether it's more of a personal grievance tour — remains to be seen.
  • A former HHS official said that after Republicans' midterm wipeout, Means is "highlighting that one of the more popular aspects of Trump's domestic agenda should be something [the administration] spends more time on to prepare the party for 2028."

The intrigue: The MAHA base sees incoming chief of staff Stephen Miller as an ally, even though he hasn't said much about movement priorities like cleaning up the food supply, curbing food additives or scrutinizing vaccines.

  • Miller's wife, Katie, hosted Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on her podcast and has posted photos of dishes with ingredients like raw milk, per the Washington Sun.
  • Means told "Face the Nation" that Miller understands corporate influence over health care and that he represents a break from Wiles.
  • "Stephen Miller has been nothing short of a champion in Making America Healthy Again. As a father of four, Miller is acutely aware of the importance of transforming our food, health, and scientific systems for the next generation of Americans," Schuster said.

Zoom in: Means, who resigned from his senior adviser post late last month, grew up in Washington and interned in George W. Bush's White House and at the Heritage Foundation before going on to work as a consultant to beverage and drug industries.

  • He told Axios in 2024 that his mother's preventable death from a chronic disease in 2021 prompted him and his sister, "functional medicine" physician and health influencer Casey Means, to advocate and work to reverse the chronic disease crisis. The siblings wrote a best-selling book called "Good Energy."
  • Calley Means also co-founded Truemed, a company that helps people buy wellness equipment using money in health savings accounts, retaining an interest while advising Kennedy, per the New York Times.

Means is widely credited with facilitating the alliance between Kennedy and President Trump in the summer of 2024 and became a special government employee in the new Trump administration.

  • He made frequent, at times flamboyant appearances in public forums, railing against a "crisis of trust" in health care institutions and claiming at one 2025 Axios event that Kennedy "has a spiritual mandate" from voters to reform broken government institutions.
  • Means' sister was tapped by Trump to be surgeon general, only to see the nomination withdrawn in April amid questions over whether she could win over enough Republican senators to be confirmed. Calley Means at the time blamed Senate health committee Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) for delay tactics.

What we're watching: It's not clear what role Means will play outside the administration — or whether his turnabout has helped or hurt the MAHA cause.

  • Key initiatives like developing a definition for ultra-processed foods remain unfinished, and the Food and Drug Administration appears to be taking a more conciliatory stance toward drug developers and other industries it regulates.

item.title: The blue wave's tough-on-crime surprise
item.description:
Democrats swept into power last week as voters also embraced tougher criminal penalties and restrictions on bail.

Why it matters: Six years after the George Floyd protests, Democrats won big without promising a return to sweeping 2020-era reforms. Some even adopted border-security rhetoric associated with Republicans.

  • Democrats gained at least 12 state legislative chambers and won governorships in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas.

By the numbers: Voters approved all six statewide ballot measures Ballotpedia tracked that proposed tougher sentences, criminal penalties or bail restrictions in 2026.

  • Five passed Nov. 3 in Indiana, Louisiana, Tennessee and Colorado. Alabama approved the sixth in May.
  • Four expanded when courts could deny or restrict bail. Two increased penalties, including for fentanyl offenses and child sex trafficking.

The shift: Some Democratic winners embraced tougher border-security language while opposing Trump's immigration crackdown.

  • Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico called himself a "border security Democrat," criticized former President Biden for failing to secure the border and said there needs to be comprehensive immigration reform.
  • Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive, said days before the election: "We needed tougher border security." He also criticized Trump's use of ICE.

Zoom in: Colorado voters backed Democrats, tougher penalties and limits on federal immigration enforcement.

  • That included electing Phil Weiser (D) as governor and approving tougher fentanyl penalties and life without parole for child sex trafficking.
  • They rejected a measure requiring police to notify federal immigration authorities in certain cases involving violent crime suspects or people with prior felony convictions whose immigration status was unlawful or uncertain.
  • Weiser and state Democrats are now weighing changes to the fentanyl measure, arguing it falls short on promised addiction treatment.

Yes, but: Virginia voters approved automatically restoring voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release from incarceration.

Zoom out: Ballotpedia's historical analysis found more punitive sentencing and bail proposals dominated from 2022 through 2026, reversing 2012–2020, when less punitive measures appeared more often.

  • Meanwhile, the nation's violent-crime rate plunged 9.7% in 2025, its steepest annual decline in 90 years. The murder rate fell 18.5%, according to the FBI.

item.title: Scoop: El Salvador blasts U.S. State Dept. over Haiti gang war
item.description:
State Department officials have quietly raised objections to El Salvador's gang-fighting efforts in Haiti — even as President Trump has offered his full support, according to diplomatic notes and informed sources.

  • On Monday, El Salvador issued a formal rebuke that questioned the "credibility" of the top U.S. diplomat in Haiti.

Why it matters: The controversy exposes the tension between Trump's MAGA foreign policy objectives and the professional diplomatic establishment in the State Department.

  • "There is a class of bureaucrats who don't want to see the change in the Western Hemisphere that POTUS wants," a U.S. official told Axios.

Zoom in: Haiti is a failed state racked by extreme corruption and gang violence despite years of international efforts, including the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) that El Salvador and other nations have backed.

  • Four Salvadoran aviation technicians supporting medical evacuations were captured Oct. 18 by gangs that refused to heed the entreaties of El Salvador's President Nayib Bukele to return the men or their bodies.
  • Bukele responded by surging special forces units to Haiti after receiving the blessing of Trump, an ally, on Oct. 27, Axios first reported.
  • "You have to do what you have to do," Trump told Bukele, who proceeded to launch military operations that resulted in firefights with gangs in the streets of Port-Au-Prince.

Friction point: Tensions between State Department officials and El Salvador erupted after an Oct. 31 gang attack on a Salvadoran convoy of five armored personnel carriers near the U.S. embassy, which was struck by gunfire.

  • On Nov. 3, Salvadoran attack helicopters repelled gangs attacking GSF soldiers from Chad, Bukele posted on X.

The next day, U.S. Chargé d'Affaires David Howell complained in a text message to Haitian Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé that El Salvador wasn't "coordinating" with the GSF.

  • "They took at least three casualties. They don't have a medical plan. They nearly killed GSF troops as I understand it," according to a copy of the text message shared with Axios.
  • Howell asked the prime minister to tell El Salvador's defense ministry to stop operations "as soon as possible ... until they coordinate. They are going to kill [GSF] troops or civilians and or get themselves killed."
  • El Salvador later accused Howell of spreading misinformation.

On Nov. 5, the U.S. embassy in San Salvador sent a formal protest in a diplomatic note to Bukele's government, saying that the U.S. "strongly opposes this lack of coordination by Salvadoran military personnel," the document shown to Axios says.

  • The note said El Salvador's "failure to coordinate" endangered the GSF and that "Salvadoran small arms fire" struck the U.S. embassy, "nearly hitting U.S. personnel."

Behind the scenes: Bukele was infuriated by the so-called "dipnote," a source said.

  • "His attitude was, 'What the f*ck? I checked with Trump. He said do what we have to do, and some bureaucrat is fighting this?' " said a source who spoke with Bukele.
  • State Department officials said it was unclear who authorized the diplomatic note and didn't comment about Howell's correspondence to Haiti's prime minister.

On Monday, Bukele's government fired back at Howell and the State Department officials. El Salvador's diplomatic note provided a point-by-point rebuttal with 4 "clarifications:"

  1. Regarding the gunfire that hit the embassy, El Salvador's ministry of foreign affairs wrote that its troops essentially had their backs to the building and were firing away from it.
  • "It is ruled out that the fire from the Salvadoran personnel struck the facilities of the American Embassy," El Salvador wrote.

2. During the attack on troops from Chad, El Salvador wrote, "Salvadoran personnel repelled the attack. It is ruled out that the fire of the Salvadoran elements was directed toward the position of Chad."

3. El Salvador also said that since Oct. 26, its armed forces repeatedly have coordinated "air assets" with the GSF and Haitian officials.

4. In its most caustic reply, El Salvador said it "categorically denies" Howell's claim that three of its soldiers were casualties.

  • "The fact that false information has been disseminated on a matter of such gravity, without providing any evidence to support it, generates serious doubts about the credibility of the rest of the assertions contained in the aforementioned report, which likewise lack any type of evidence that would allow their accuracy to be verified," the note said.

What they're saying: An official spokesperson for El Salvador couldn't be reached. Haiti's prime minister didn't return messages seeking comment.

  • A State Department official insisted that "three Salvadorans were injured ... one of which was serious enough to have been medevaced outside the country for additional treatment."
  • A source close to El Salvador's government showed Axios a picture of the smiling soldier with a leg brace on and said he was flown out of Haiti because there were no adequate medical facilities, not because the injury was serious.
  • The State Department, echoing comments from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Sunday, said it appreciates El Salvador's efforts, "but the Trump administration has also been clear on the need to deconflict anti-gang operations to ensure seamless implementation of President Trump's policy to support efforts to free Haiti from gangs."

item.title: How Nvidia's crisis and politics could deliver the pause AI leaders want
item.description:
A political backlash against AI and data centers — now compounded by a crisis facing the technology's most influential champion — could help force a slowdown that industry leaders have struggled to achieve voluntarily.

Why it matters: Tapping the brakes on AI development — which frontier AI developers claim to want but have so far failed to do given the risk of offering an advantage to a competitor — could give society more time to prepare for economic upheaval and the risks of superintelligent systems.

  • A wave of Democratic victories and data center moratoriums is now joined by a potentially weakened Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who admitted to having a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.
  • Huang, who has led the industry in barreling through past resistance to AI acceleration, may be less able to do so while under a microscope.
  • While both factors could stymie data center expansion in the U.S., it's far from clear that would slow AI's advance.

Between the lines: Huang has been a powerful counterweight to calls for AI restraint, dismissing fears of an AI bubble or purported catastrophic risks to humanity from the technology.

  • An investigation — by the board, an ascendant Democratic Congress or federal authorities — could curb his ability to make the case for continued expansion, leaving an opening for those calling for more restrictions.
  • Nvidia says Huang will remain CEO and the news won't slow the company, but the potential impact on his political influence is hard to measure.
  • The fallout extends beyond that. Nvidia is both the dominant supplier of AI chips and an investor in companies building AI infrastructure. A crisis that raises questions about its leadership, business practices or financial relationships could ripple through the industry's expansion plans.

The intrigue: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all warned about the potentially catastrophic risks of advanced AI, with all expressing, at times, the need to slow or pace the development of advanced AI.

  • But the competitive race has made it difficult for any one company to hit the brakes without risking falling behind rivals or China in a high-stakes race for supremacy.

What they're saying: Anthony Aguirre, CEO of the Future of Life Institute, says a slowdown in data center construction would be welcome, even if it wouldn't accomplish nearly as much as more direct restrictions on frontier AI development.

  • "I'll take whatever I can get," Aguirre told Axios in an interview. Aguirre and a number of other researchers have long seen the development of increasingly powerful AI as an existential threat.
  • But he is skeptical that slowing data center construction alone would buy society an additional year or two, given the vast computing resources companies already possess and the growing ability of AI systems to help improve themselves.
  • Aguirre said the bigger opportunity may be political: Resistance to data centers could help generate momentum for legislation and regulation that more directly limits the development of potentially dangerous AI systems.

The big picture: Aguirre argues that the goal shouldn't simply be to delay superintelligence by a year or two, but to reconsider whether humanity should build it at all.

  • He favors a "pause and pivot" toward AI systems designed to augment human abilities rather than replace them.
  • Other researchers and executives favor continued development with stronger safeguards, reflecting a broader debate over how much restraint is necessary and what form it should take.

Yes, but: Slowing data center construction in the U.S. doesn't necessarily mean slowing AI progress globally.

  • Meta and other companies are exploring data center construction outside the U.S. Google announced a plan last week to invest $15 billion over two years in Malaysia.
  • And Chinese AI developers wouldn't face the same U.S. restrictions, potentially allowing them to narrow the gap with American competitors.

The other side: The threat from China isn't as straightforward as it appears.

  • Chinese AI companies benefit in part from distillation of leading American models and technical knowledge developed in the U.S., Aguirre said. Slowing the American frontier could therefore have some effect on China's pace as well.
  • A U.S. decision to slow frontier development could open the door to direct conversations with China about mutually pacing the technology, rather than treating superintelligence as an unavoidable arms race.

The bottom line: The AI industry is hoping to overcome political resistance and keep building. Advocates of slowing frontier AI see an opportunity to turn that resistance into something bigger: a chance to reconsider not just how fast AI should advance, but how far it should go.

item.title: The new battle for Congress: Trump's veto
item.description:
Democrats will charge into January with a sweeping mandate — but as President Trump has repeatedly noted, his veto power can deliver a robust roadblock to his opponents' agenda.

Why it matters: Democrats may be forced to compromise to get legislative priorities through. Trump will have to decide how frequently he'll use the power — and whether he'll strike down bills popular among Americans.

State of play: Democrats have secured 54 seats in the upcoming Senate, per the AP's projections, and are leading in two tight races in Mississippi and Alaska that have yet to be called.

  • In the House, they've won 254, per AP, with several race calls still to come.
  • Neither majority will be large enough to cross the two-thirds threshold Democrats would need to override a presidential veto on their own.

Friction point: Trump knows that — and has teased his plans to impede Democrats' progress by using the power liberally.

  • On Tuesday night, as election results rolled in, Trump posted an image of a red MAGA-esque hat that read "VETO" in all caps. A similar hat was displayed on the Resolute Desk during a Thursday signing ceremony.
  • Asked on Fox News how he'd work with a Democratic Congress, Trump pointed to the veto: "They're in control, but they're really not in control because they can send over, you know, 50 different great bills that they're all excited about and I send them back with a nice stamp, veto."
  • White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement provided to Axios that Trump is "willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans."
  • She added, "If Democrats choose to pursue radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

Worth noting: Lawmakers secured enough support to override a Trump veto across party lines during his first term on the National Defense Authorization Act in 2021.

Yes, but: While Trump could use veto threats to force lawmakers to negotiate or to halt legislation altogether, vetoing popular measures could benefit Democrats' messaging for 2028, when a potential trifecta in all three branches of government would let them enact their agenda with little interference.

  • Responding to an image of Trump's "VETO" hat Thursday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wrote, "If Donald Trump wants to be Mr. Veto, let's test that out. The new Democratic majority in Congress should pass bills to make life more affordable and our government less corrupt."
  • But doing so will still require coalition-building on the Hill, says Jonathan Lewallen, an associate professor at the University of Tampa who has studied policy agenda-setting and veto threats.
  • He highlights two key issue areas where Trump has already threatened vetoes in the first half of his administration that Democrats have pledged to tackle: defense policy and consumer protection.

Yes, but: "There may come a point in the next two years where Trump is still issuing lots of veto threats and potentially even vetoing the occasional bill, and it just becomes less effective as a strategy," Lewallen says.

  • That means the administration might instead use another tactic with legislation they disagree with: quietly letting them become law automatically after 10 days without Trump's signature.

The bottom line: Reversing Trump's agenda from Capitol Hill isn't expected to be smooth sailing.

  • But winning back control of both chambers isn't just about passing bills, with Dem-led investigations, hearings and subpoenas expected on the horizon.

Go deeper: House Republicans vote to sustain Trump vetoes

item.title: AI stocks bounce back — with one notable exception
item.description:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang.

The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom.

By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year.

Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception.

  • Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared.
  • The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.)
  • Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%.
  • Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July.

Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia.

  • Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future.

The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals.

  • Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year.
  • Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday.

Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch.

  • "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday.
  • "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night.
  • "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday.

These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips.

  • And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors.

The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off.

  • For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat.
  • Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors.

What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance?

  • Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce?
item.content:encoded:
Data: FactSet; Chart: Matt Phillips/Axios

The AI trade has regained momentum despite — or maybe because of — Nvidia's struggles following the weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang.

The big picture: Monday's sudden burst of exuberance for AI was the latest wide swing for a market upended by last week's "blue tsunami" in the midterm elections and the threat they could pose to the data center boom.

By the numbers: The Nasdaq 100 index of large-cap technology shares soared 3.4%, its biggest daily jump since late March and its second-best showing of the year.

Zoom in: Stocks romped across the AI ecosystem — well, with one important exception.

  • Pick-and-shovel plays such as engineering and construction companies, and makers of data center inputs like fiberoptic cables, servers and data storage devices soared.
  • The companies that build and lease out data center computing power, known as neoclouds, also jumped. (Those companies had been at the epicenter of recent jitters about financing for the AI boom.)
  • Hyperscalers rose, paced by Meta, which notched a gain of 5.1%.
  • Semiconductors roared, with the SOX index posting its best gain — 6.9% — since late July.

Yes, but: The glaring exception to the AI-palooza was its best-known player, Nvidia.

  • Weekend revelations from CEO Jensen Huang — who acknowledged having an affair with a woman suspected of connections to Chinese intelligence — left investors grappling with uncertainty about the CEO's future.

The intrigue: Some investors may see Nvidia's pain as potential gain for rivals.

  • Broadcom jumped 8.8%, its best day in nearly a year.
  • Advanced Micro Devices soared 13.3%, benefiting also from an upgrade to "Outperform" — effectively, a "buy" recommendation — from Oppenheimer analysts on Sunday.

Context: Bullish commentary from Wall Street established the background music for Monday's big bounce, as analysts urged investors to buy into the market's recent soft patch.

  • "We believe stocks are now clearly in oversold territory," Goldman Sachs analysts wrote in a note Monday.
  • "We believe the market's reaction to the midterms is overdone," wrote Morgan Stanley tech analysts in a note entitled "Buy the Drop: AI Investment Opportunities Post the U.S. Midterms," which it published Sunday night.
  • "We do not think AI is a continued sell here. In fact, tech drawdown is offering certain opportunities. The selloff was very sharp," JPMorgan equity strategists wrote Monday.

These analysts could be right. The recent slump has been deep in certain sectors such as chips.

  • And buying the dip has been a solid strategy in recent years, especially for retail investors.

The other side: On the other hand, there may be good reasons such stocks sold off.

  • For example, even before the news about the Nvidia CEO or the anti-data center vote at the polls, Wall Street expectations for capital expenditures from hyperscalers had been looking a bit flat.
  • Given that a large percentage of that AI investment is spent on the semiconductors needed to make these computing centers, well, compute, that would seem to be important for tech investors.

What's next: Will the stock market's rally be the start of a new phase of AI exuberance?

  • Or is it just an example of Wall Street's proverbial dead cat bounce?

item.title: House Dems size up 2028 Senate map after midterm landslide
item.description:
Current and former House Democrats, flush with victory following their landslide midterm wins, are already looking at potential opportunities to run for Senate in 2028, Axios has learned.

Why it matters: Democrats' 2026 romp — with wins in Texas, South Carolina, Kansas and possibly even Mississippi — has some party members reevaluating what were once considered impossible targets.

  • A source close to Rep. Sharice Davids (D-Kan.) — who was reelected by 21 percentage points in a district former Vice President Harris carried by four points in 2024 — did not rule out her running against Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).
  • "All options are on the table," the source said, adding that Davids' "focus right now is on delivering actual results and overcoming the chaos from these extreme policies we're seeing."
  • Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) was defeated by Democrat Adam Hamilton last week, marking the first time in nearly a century a Democrat has been elected to the U.S. Senate from Kansas.

North Carolina: Rep. Don Davis is "taking a look at" a run against Republican Sen. Ted Budd, a source familiar with his thinking told Axios.

  • Davis won a third term on Tuesday after defeating his GOP opponent in a district President Trump carried by 12 points in 2024. Republicans redrew the district with the express goal of ensuring Davis' loss.
  • Former Rep. Wiley Nickel, who was elected Wake County district attorney on Tuesday, would consider a Senate run if state Attorney General Jeff Jackson doesn't, a source close to him told Axios. The two served together in the House.
  • Democratic former Gov. Roy Cooper won North Carolina's other U.S. Senate seat last week in a nearly 20-percentage-point landslide over Republican Michael Whatley.

Pennsylvania: A huge field of Democrats is gearing up to potentially run for the seat held by Democratic Sen. John Fetterman.

  • Fetterman, who has morphed from a populist firebrand to an arch-centrist, has angered much of the party by siding with Republicans on key votes.
  • Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) told Axios in a statement: "I am thinking hard about my next steps and will be having that conversation with my family and supporters."
  • Said former Rep. Susan Wild: "I am not ruling anything out at this time. ... I think PA is long overdue for a woman senator, and that will factor into my eventual decision."

Florida: State Rep. Angie Nixon is already hinting at a 2028 run against Republican Sen. Ashley Moody after losing to her on Tuesday by three percentage points.

  • But some in the party's centrist wing believe Nixon's left-wing politics and her affiliation with the Democratic Socialists of America may have cost her in a Democratic wave year and are looking to recruit elsewhere.
  • Rep. Jared Moskowitz (D-Fla.), who won reelection in a district Trump carried by nine points in 2024 and is often mentioned as a potential candidate for statewide office, is in the mix, sources said.
  • Sources also pointed to Rep. Kathy Castor (D-Fla.), who won in a district that went for Trump by 11 points, as another possible candidate. A Castor spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

item.title: France says Iranian hackers sabotaged supermarket refrigerators
item.description:
The French government has blamed an Iranian military hacking unit for cyberattacks that disrupted refrigeration systems at roughly 700 grocery stores and other retail locations last month, causing food losses and at least 15 fires.

Why it matters: The attacks underscore how Iranian government hackers are moving beyond stealing data and disrupting websites to manipulating the physical equipment that keeps essential services running.

Driving the news: France's Ministry for Europe and Foreign Affairs attributed the Oct. 11–12 attacks to Iran on Monday, calling them the country's first cyberattack campaign conducted purely for sabotage on French territory.

  • The government's Cyber Crisis Coordination Center specifically attributed the attacks to Shahid Kaveh, a hacking unit within Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
  • Hackers manipulated refrigeration equipment to raise temperatures, causing tens of millions of euros in food losses and at least 15 fires, according to French officials.
  • The same operation also targeted equipment at small hydroelectric facilities in France, with limited effects, according to an intelligence report.

Yes, but: The French government has not publicly attributed a separate wave of refrigeration attacks that occurred last week to the same hackers.

Zoom in: French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to several online hacktivist personas, including CyberAveng3rs and Soldiers of Solomon, that publicly claim responsibility for the unit's operations.

  • Investigators found that infrastructure used in the refrigeration attacks was also used to scan industrial equipment using techniques previously associated with Shahid Kaveh.
  • They also found traces of Farsi in the attack infrastructure and identified a propaganda outlet linked to the unit that publicized the attack.

The big picture: Iran has a history of targeting industrial equipment in cyber operations, including American water systems and Israeli refrigeration equipment.

  • French intelligence linked Shahid Kaveh to attacks on Israeli refrigeration equipment earlier this year and a 2023 campaign targeting industrial controllers manufactured by Unitronics.

What to watch: France plans to summon Iran's ambassador and propose new European Union sanctions against Iranian individuals and entities involved in the attacks.

item.title: Sex, secrets and spies: The history of suspected honey traps
item.description:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a woman suspected of spying for China echoes past controversies involving prominent Americans whose romantic relationships raised national security concerns.

Why it matters: Foreign intelligence operatives can use romantic relationships to gain access to political intelligence, corporate secrets and classified information — posing serious national security risks.

Driving the news: Jensen Huang acknowledged an extramarital affair in a message to employees Sunday, following reports that he had a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

  • Per The New York Times, U.S. authorities suspected China's Ministry of State Security of recruiting Alice Huang to seek information about Jensen Huang and influence his feelings about selling AI chips to Chinese firms.
  • Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. China has also denied the allegations.

Zoom out: The evidence of foreign intelligence involvement varies, with some cases involving actual security breaches, while others raised concerns about possible foreign spying.

Read more below.

Jensen Huang

State of play: Reports about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang have raised questions about whether Chinese intelligence gained access to Nvidia's secrets or sought to influence its business decisions.

  • AFP and Reuters photos showed them together in 2024 and 2025.
  • Employees reported seeing Jensen Huang at Megaspeed's offices, where Alice Huang worked as an executive, according to Culper Research, a short-seller that published a report on Nvidia's China business in May 2026.
  • An employee told Culper that Jensen and Alice had a "very close" relationship.

What's next: Three Republican House committee chairs have requested a briefing with Huang about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards against foreign threats.

James J. Smith and Katrina Leung

A 2006 DOJ report found that counterintelligence agent James J. Smith had a secret 18-year affair with Katrina Leung, an FBI informant who was suspected of passing information onto China.

  • The investigation found that Leung had provided classified U.S. government information to China without FBI authorization, exposing major failures in the bureau's oversight of informants.
  • A DOJ inspector general investigation also found that Leung had an affair with another FBI agent, William Cleveland.
  • Smith and Leung were arrested in 2003. Both ultimately pleaded guilty to making false statements, rather than espionage charges.

Maria Butina and Paul Erickson

Russian activist-turned-politician Maria Butina pleaded guilty in 2018 to conspiring to act as an unregistered agent of the Russian government after becoming romantically involved with Republican operative Paul Erickson.

  • Federal prosecutors withdrew the allegation that she traded sex for political access, saying they misinterpreted the evidence, per ABC News.
  • Prosecutors maintained that Butina used her relationship with Erickson to conceal activities intended to advance Russian interests, according to ABC News.

Eric Swalwell and Christine Fang

FBI records declassified in August 2026 show former Congressman Eric Swalwell acknowledged having sexual encounters with a suspected Chinese operative, Christine Fang, per the Washington Post.

  • According to the records, Swalwell said the interactions were casual and that they never formally dated.

Flashback: In 2020, Axios uncovered that Fang had targeted politicians in California, including Swalwell.

  • According to reports, Fang participated in fundraising for Swalwell's campaign and helped place an intern in his office.
  • Intelligence officials told Axios at the time that Fang gained access to political power through fundraising, networking, personal charisma, and romantic or sexual relationships with at least two Midwestern mayors, too.
  • The FBI never accused Swalwell of wrongdoing in connection with his relationship with Fang, per the Washington Post.

Benjamin Bishop

In 2014, defense contractor Benjamin Pierce Bishop pleaded guilty to disclosing classified information to a Chinese woman with whom he had a romantic relationship, according to the Department of Justice.

  • Bishop was sentenced to more than seven years in prison for disclosing classified national defense information and unlawfully retaining classified documents.
  • According to the DOJ, Bishop, a former Army lieutenant colonel, retrieved a classified photograph of a Chinese naval asset at his girlfriend's request.

item.title: Trump: New Iran attacks "quite unlikely"
item.description:
President Trump said Monday that a renewed military campaign against Iran is "quite unlikely" and "doesn't seem to be necessary."

Why it matters: Trump stopped short of saying the war was over, but his comments on Truth Social and at an impromptu press conference were the furthest he went in that direction since February.

  • Trump made his comments less than a week after conceding that the war was one of the reasons Republicans lost the midterm elections.

Driving the news: The president in recent days has been weighing three options: launch new strikes, continue to strangle Iran's regime economically, or cut a deal that includes significant concessions to the Iranians.

  • Trump signaled on Monday that he's going with the strangle strategy for now. That means keeping up the "status quo" — continuing the naval blockade, in addition to a new operation dubbed "Iron Gate" to cut off land routes that Iran uses to move advanced weaponry and other technology.
  • Trump said the war is "effectively over" militarily. But he added that he doesn't want to formally announce that before he makes sure U.S. allies in the region are safe.
  • "We have great allies and we have to make sure they are not hurt. We want a long-term solution," Trump said.

State of play: Trump made his comments hours after meeting with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdul Rahman Al Thani about the negotiations with Iran.

  • "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo" to resuming the war, Trump said.
  • The Qatari prime minister also met separately with Vice President Vance, who's been leading the Iran talks for the administration in recent weeks. Al Thani wrote on X that he discussed with Trump ways "to progress the U.S.-Iran talks."
  • "Grateful for the positive discussions on reaching a deal and bringing peace to the region," he added.
  • A diplomat briefed on the details of the meeting said Trump made clear to Al Thani that he wants a deal and will give negotiations a chance. But he also noted that if Iranians don't take negotiations seriously, he could reverse course, the diplomat said.

What he is saying: "Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is locked and loaded and ready to go. At this point, however, that seems to be quite unlikely," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

  • "We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America's interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure," he added.

What to watch: Trump said that Iran is "talking very politely" with the U.S. and noted that there is a "good chance that could get ended," seemingly referring to the military conflict.

  • "Hope we are gonna be able to make a deal with them," he added.

The other side: Iran's Supreme National Security Council secretary, Mohsen Rezaei, wrote on X shortly after Trump made his comments that the war "has wrecked the U.S. government."

  • He called Trump comments about negotiations with Iran "imaginary" and called on the U.S. "to SURRENDER" to Iran's conditions for ending the war.

What we're watching: Oil prices have eased in recent weeks amid optimism that combat will end. Brent crude oil futures dropped to $92 on Monday.
